speechtext: Just as I entered the House this afternoon my attention was directed to an extraordinary despatch which appears in today's Ottawa Citizen, and which purports to emanate from Toronto. ' It is as follows:

speakerposition: subtopic

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Toronto, June 13.-Rev. Dr. Chown, general superintendent, informed the Methodist conference yesterday morning that he had sent letters to Ottawa declaring the position of the Methodist church on race track gambling.
Rev. Dr. Speer stated that letters were of no avail in this case, "but money in the lobby. We hadn't the money. I hope the department did something. It was a foregone conclusion that these men of the race track would get what they wanted."
As far as my knowledge goes, and according to my firm conviction, the suggestion or implication contained in the words of Dr. Speer, if he is correctly reported, is a most outrageous and scandalous libel.
Some hon. M,EMBERS: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext:
I sincerely hope he is not correctly reported. Since my return to Parliament some five weeks ago I have not seen a race track man around the

lobby of this House, and I have not heard of one being here.

subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext:
The reflection
upon Parliament by this gentleman, if he is correctly reported, is so serious that I thought it my duty to mention the matter openly and publicly, and to request His Honour the Speaker to consider what would be the appropriate action, if action be deemed advisable, for Parliament to take jn the matter.

subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext: I also hope that the despatch is not true but so far as I am concerned I shall feel it my duty to take such action in the matter, if it be true, as will properly preserve the honour and the dignity of Parliament

subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext: Not only is the honour of members of the House of Commons involved in a statement of this character, but there is likewise involved the question of sapping and undermining public confidence in the representative institutions in a democratic country. subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.
speechtext: May I be allowed to offer a suggestion? I would ignore absolutely the fellow who indulged in such slander. To do otherwise would be giving him too much publicity. I would not bring him before the Bar of the House because that would be disgracing the bar. I would meet the statement with silent contempt.

subtopic: EXPECTED THE RACE MEN TO WIN OUT.

If this man has any data to support such a statement he should come forward and acquaint the public with it. On section 1-Short title.
I understand that this harbour used to be administered by a commission the same as the harbour of Three Rivers-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's remarks are not in order on clause 1, which is merely the "short title" of the Bill.

For once you are right, Mr. Chairman, I apologize. I thought it was clause 2.
Section agreed to
On section 2-Property and rights vested in His Majesty.

1 understand that the harbour of Pictou has heretofore been administered by a commission in the same way as the harbour of Three Rivers, and that hereafter all liabilities and! expenditures are to be assumed by the Government, and that a department of the Government is to administer the harbour. Will there be any particular officer in Pictou to look after that administration? Will the Government hereafter eharge any wharfage or dockage dues

to ships using this harbour, or will it be treated the same as our other harbours? Or is the fact? that it is going to be administered by the 'Government an indication that the Government will assume the responsibility of improving the harbour without charging the expenditure against the harbour itself, this expenditure being paid from the Dominion Treasury? If that be the case, I would ask tke minister to put the harbour of Three Rivers in the same position, because we require a lot of improvements there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has judged the situation correctly. The revenue from the port of Pictou has been decreasing year by year until at the present time the expenditure is about $450 in excess of the revenue. It is not the intention of the Government to undertake any new work there; the purpose of this Bill is simply to transfer the administration of the port from the Harbour Commission to the Department of Public Works. There have been many precedents for this action, and the transfer will not involve any extra expense to the Government that I can see. The question of liabilities was raised when the resolution was under discussion some weeks ago, and I have since ascertained that the Harbour Commission does not owe any money, but will be turning over to the department, if this Bill passes, about $186. With regard to the very important port of Three Rivers, I shall be very glad to give every consideration to the suggestion made by the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. Bureau).
Have you an estimate of how much money will be required to put the harbour of Pictou in good shape?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As far as I understand, no expenditure will be necessary, the wharves being in a sufficiently good state of repair at the present time.
Are any repairs asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.

I accept my hon. friend's word, for I know he is a business man and understands the value of figures. But, Mr. Chairman, I view with alarm the taking over by the Government of any of these public works. I have been surprised of late to receive from a firm of brokers a circular wherein the name of the Dominion is being paraded as endorsing the scheme for the improvement of the harbour of St.

John. It will be remembered that this harbour was taken over by the Government, but how I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has not been taken over yet.
Bonds are being issued to meet the expenditure on the harbour works, and those bonds are endorsed by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question?

I will conclude if my hon. friend pleases. I notice that those bonds are endorsed by the Dominion, and the name of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell), as Acting Minister of Public Works, is made use of in that circular. I have the greatest possible objection to the credit of the Dominion being used to assist enterprises of this nature. The public will be surprised when it. becomes known that the treasury is being involved to the extent of millions of dollars for the St. John harbour improvements. I do not know if this has escaped the attention of the Government, but I was appalled when I saw that our national credit was being pledged in that way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. minister replies-and I think a reply would now be quite in order-I take it for granted that this reference to the harbour of St. John is only by way of comparison.
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Because it will be entirely out of order to enter into a general discussion concerning the harbour of St. John in connection with this Bill.

I am afraid of the prospect of any further dealings with harbour commissions in the Maritime Provinces. We were assured when the subject of the St. John harbour works was before the House that everything was above board. Now we find that gentlemen at St. John are selling harbour bonds,-and it is quite easy for them to get the money when the name of the Dominion appears as the guarantor of those bonds. We are taxed beyond the human limit, and the people of this country are quite willing to be so taxed, but only in a legitimate way, and they will not tolerate any such incursions on the Government Exchequer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is true that a
year ago authority was given by Parliament for the taking over, under conditions clear-

ly specified in legislation introduced for that purpose, of the port of St. John and placing it under a commission. But effect could be given to that legislation only after the city of St. John held a referendum in which the majority of the people declared themselves in favour of nationalizing the port and placing it under a commission. Such a referendum has not yet been held; therefore the port has not. been nationalized-

Has my hon. friend
seen the circular-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Just allow me to finish. The Government, accordingly, did not guarantee any of the debentures for the city of St. John, so far as my knowledge goes. They will do so only after a referendum is taken and the harbour passes under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Marine. At present the city of St. John do their own financing for the port; the Dominion Government do not guarantee any of their debentures.

When the resolution was before the committee I asked why special treatment was given in this particular case. For instance, I have a communication from residents of Fabre, on lake Timiskaming, who claim that their dock was damaged by the ice last winter and that they have been obliged to land their goods on the shore; yet they are paying wharfage dues. Why are these people treated differently from the people of Pictou? What is the policy of the Government in regard to wharves where dues are being paid but where the necessary accommodation is not being furnished? Will it be necessary for the minister to bring in a Bill for each one?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This procedure has been followed on more than one occasion. For instance, under my predecessor, Sir Douglas Hazen, the harbour of North Sydney was transferred from the Department of Marine to the Department of Public Works. I mention only this instance now, but I could cite many other similar cases. I would suggest that my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) should write me in regard to the particular harbour that he speaks about. If the revenue there is not sufficient to keep the wharf in a satisfactory state of repair, it would be quite in order for me to bring the matter to the attention of this House, as has been done in the case of Pictou harbour.

If this Bill passes will the business of the port be conducted by the harbour master or by an engineer of the
Department of Public Works when repairs are necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The business of the harbour will be conducted by the harbour master, who will be under the Public Works Department.

I would like to know definitely from the minister what the policy of the Government will be after the authority which has hitherto been vested in harbour commissions has been done away with. How will the works that are now in existence be maintained? Under present conditions, whatever money these commissioners get is used for the building of wharves and breakwaters and their maintenance, as well as a little dredging. The minister mentioned the harbour of North Sydney. We have a few works in that harbour which were built by the commission. The breakwater near the north end of the harbour is so old that I cannot tell the minister whether it was 'built by the commission or not. I do know that while the commission were in existence they used to repair the breakwater and keep it in shape. During the last two years, since the commission went out of existence, the whole of the harbour and its works have been under the control of the Government, and I have been instructed by men interested in the conditions at North Sydney that this breakwater, which is a very useful structure, affording protection to the whole harbour and particularly to the coal and iron ore piers of the Nova Scotia Steel Company, is falling into decay or disrepair. Very little money will keep it in repair, but if it is broken up or destroyed by the action of the sea it will cost a great deal to put it in good condition. I bring this matter to the notice of the minister with a view to his seeing that this useful breakwater is not allowed to be brokqn up or destroyed.

I wish to 'bring to the
attention of the minister a matter I have already taken up with his- department and to ask that before the Bill is finally passed the request I am going to make be given consideration. Owing to the increased tax on alcohol, the cost to hospitals will be considerably increased. I am informed by the Vancouver General Hospital, for instance, and the same will be true in varying degree of all hospitals, I presume, that the increased tax will result in additional cost to that one hospital, which is a very large institution, of upwards of $3,000 per annum. As there are many hospitals, the cost will



be increased to them very, very materially in the aggregate. I would suggest to the minister that when the Bill is brought down it should contain a provision that spirits used exclusively in hospitals for medicinal purposes shall be exempt from taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: My hon. friend will doubtless appreciate the difficulties that face the department in the control of alcohol after it leaves the distillery. It is quite true that under the present Act alcohol used for any purposes whatsoever and whether it went to hospitals or elsewhere would have to pay the excise duty of $2.40 a gallon. When it was proposed to amend the Act last year there was quite a strong appeal made by the various hospitals and by scientific laboratories in the country to have alcohol which was used in hospitals and in laboratories for research purposes exempted from the tax. The matter has been given some consideration. In respect to the particular point my hon. friend raises I may say that to grant his request would in effect be giving the hospitals another form of subsidy. With the additional duty of $2 hospitals will pay for the alcohol they use for medicinal purposes a duty of $4.40 a gallon. It is quite true that if the additional $2 was not imposed in the case of hospitals, or if the whole excise tax was not imposed in their case, it would be a great benefit to the hospitals, *but it would, of course, entail that much loss of revenue to the Government. In effect, therefore, it would be giving the hospitals a subsidy. Let us assume for the sake of argument that the excise duty paid by the Vancouver General Hospital to which my hon. friend has referred, on the alcohol it used during the year was a little over $2,000. To meet my hon. friend's request would simply mean that the treasury of this country would be practically foregoing $2,000 for the benefit of that hospital. It is an arguable point whether hospitals should be subsidized by the noncollection of that revenue. It is a question whether the additional money required for the payment of that alcohol should be given as a direct subsidy by the Government or should be subscribed by those who at the present time support the hospital. I need hardly say that I have a great deal of sympathy personally with the view expressed by my hon. friend, and which has been put before the department from many different sources in Canada. I shall be quite willing to give the matter fuller consideration before the Bill is brought,down. In the meantime I would suggest that my hon. friend let the matter stand.

It has been represented to me that the imposition of a tax on alcohol and the numerous restrictions placed upon its use by the department have made alcohol very expensive and have hampered scientific men in their investigations requiring its use. I am not familiar enough with the subject to judge whether these criticisms are valid or not, but I just wish to direct the minister's attention to this matter, which has been called to my attention by a college professor, and I should like to know if there is any reason for the imposition of these restrictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
My hon. friend's point
touches to some extent the point raised by *my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens). It is true that as regards commercial work we are making a great advance because under this Bill we are providing for the elimination of the excise duty on the ethyl alcohol when converted by the addition of wood alcohol into methylated spirits; but I do not think that is exactly the form of alcohol to which my hon. friend refers. The point raised by my hon. friend from, Guysborough is more in relation I think to the ethyl alcohol used for scientific purposes. It is true that it would be a great benefit to have this exempt from the tax, but I must point out the objection that exists in the case of all these exemptions from the duty, and that is in connection with releasing the alcohol from the distilleries into other people's hands in a form in which it can be used for beverage purposes. With the recently added duty the total duty on alcohol will be $5 on the imported and $4.40 excise. My hon. friend will understand the frantic desire of gentlemen of a bibulous temperament, of whom there seem to be still a great many in the country, to get hold of this alcohol, and the great difficulty of control when once out of our hands. Under the present prohibitory legislation of this country-and I am not pronouncing an opinion upon it from a moral standpoint, but simply looking at it in a cold-blooded business-like way so far as operating the department is concerned-the result has been that owing to the high and mounting costs of spirits of all kinds, where about two years ago we were only prosecuting a score or so of people for manufacturing spirits by illicit stills, the number last year amounted to nearly nine hundred, and I venture to say we have only touched the fringe. Every form of alcohol that can be used for beverage purposes becomes increasingly difficult to control directly it leaves our hands.

It cannot leave our hands until the duty is paid by the distillery but directly we give it into other people's hands to be used for different purposes, it is going to make it an exceedingly difficult matter to control. It is rather a serious question for the department to consider. As the matter stands at present I have not been disposed to grant freedom from the excise duty to ethyl alcohol used for the purpose which my hon. friend speaks of although, I repeat, we have 'made a very great concession by permitting denatured alcohol to be free of excise duty and that, I think, will give a great impetus to commercial and industrial work.
What duty does this law impose on ethyl alcohol when imported for industrial purposes and what is the excise duty on alcohol manufactured in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Methylated spirits can
only be imported by the department under the Act as it stands. The department itself, under the law, has been the sole maker and dispenser of methylated spirits. There is a duty on wood alcohol that is brought in, and, of course, on alcohol, but up to the present time we have been the sole makers and dispensers of methylated spirits. The Bill would give us the power to grant licensees the privilege of importing. On wood alcohol, the duty, I think, is twenty cents a gallon.	*
And the excise?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: There would be no excise duty on wood alcohol.
Does the department import any methylated spirits?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, we make them all. The department has been purchasing ethyl alcohol and wood alcohol, and then making the methylated spirits, the methylated spirts when ethyl and wood alcohol are mixed together being such that the alcohol is non-recoverable for drinking purposes.

No excise duty is being
paid on ethyl alcohol?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, on ethyl alcohol.
It makes the methylated ' spirit pretty high for the department to dispense?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We do not pay the duty and therefore we do not calculate the duty as being a part of the cost, but even at that it is urged that the department cannot make it as cheaply as people would be able to get it if they were allowed to go into 222J
the business of making ethyl alcohol and also methylated spirits. But there has been some dispute about that. I do not think that the anticipations some of them have as to cheaper industrial alcohol will be realized in the future. It is a somewhat difficult matter, however, to keep up to the requirements unless we enlarge our plants, and this Bill will allow others to go into the business.

What is the price of
methylated spirits?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I think we got it down as low as ninety cents a gallon one timer it is somewhere between that and $1.20. L will give my hon. friend the precise figures: in reference to this. Before the resolution is carried I might refer very briefly to one or two other provisions. There are several clauses in the resolution which very much increase the penalties in connection not only with illicitly distilling, but also with the selling of liquor illicitly distilled. Under the old Act a man who distilled without a license was only fined $100 for the first offence. This is increased to $200, it being quite manifest that if he illicitly distilled a barrel or two the product would be worth more than the fine and therefore we have thought that we ought to double up on the fine in order that he will run a very much greater risk. Similarly, under the old law, the penalty for a man who got the liquor that was "illicitly distilled and then sold it was almost nominal. The fine imposed on that man is heavier than the fine imposed on the man who illicitly distills. I think the House will be thoroughly in accord with the amendment. The resolution deals with another important matter that I would like to take up a little more explicitly when the Bill comes down and that is the complete change in the administration of the Act in respect to vinegar and acetic acid. Last year this Bill was brought up and there was very strong opposition to it on the part of certain firms who had been manufacturing acetic acid by a new process and who objected very strongly on the ground that it was a deterrent to a lot of our manufacturing processes to tax acetic acid at the rate of four cents a gallon. When the Act first came into force they charged the vinegar man not on the spirits that were used in the making of the vinegar but on the acetic acid contained in the vinegar when it was manufactured, four cents a gallon. There was another clause in the Act which imposed a duty of four cents a gallon on the acetic acid produced from wood alcohol. Subsequent to this time and

during the war there has been a process devised by which they can get acetic acid in very much greater purity from other sources and consequently we found it necessary to consider whether we should impose that four cent duty on all forms of manufactured acetic acid or leave it off altogether. On giving the matter very full consideration *we have decided to revise the method of taxing the vinegar men and we have decided to tax them on the spirits and not on the acetic acid contained in the vinegar and then to free acetic acid altogether from taxation. I think that in so far as revenue goes the thing will about balance and it will give a very great impetus to a whole lot of manufacturing processes.

Was it the manufacturers or the producers of leaf tobacco who asked for the change set forth in section 2:
That the definition of "Standard Leaf Tobacco" in paragraph "C" of Section 8 be amended so as to include the provision that "Standard Leaf Tobacco" as applied to any kind of tobacco means that which contains ten per cent or more of moisture.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is a matter that has been deemed extremely desirable by the department itself. At the present time the law in reference to standard leaf tobacco says tobacco " which contains ten per cent of water and ninety per cent of solid matter." On raw leaf tobacco that comes in some will have ten per cent of moisture, some twelve, some sixteen and some perhaps eighteen. This tobacco is tested and dried, and if it has ten per cent of moisture they are charged on ninety per cent' of tobacco; if it goes to sixteen per cent, they are allowed six per cent for moisture. If on the other hand it goes only eight per cent, they are charged on ninety-two per cent. The consequence is that it involves not only a great amount of work but results in a confused lot of tests. We have considered it would be only fair to cease the practice altogether and to say that tobacco shall be taken to mean tobacco containing ten per cent moisture and no more. If it is above ten per cent, say twelve per cent, importers are penalized to that extent. The matter will adjust itself immediately because what will happen will be that the man who is shipping tobacco will simply dry it to ten per cent. It will mean the release of a large number of our men for the purposes of other work and permit the operations of the department to be conducted expeditiously and without inconvenience to those concerned.

I may not have caught the full force of the minister's statement in regard to some sale that he mentioned. I understood him to say that he was providing against the sale of illicit liquors. I may be wrong in that but if so I think it is practically new ground for the Dominion to cover. I understood that when what we call liquors get into the shape of being commercial commodities they came under the jurisdiction of the province entirely, and that the provincial authorities would have the say as to what the punishment would be for selling anything in the shape of intoxicating liquors. I do not think that we have the power to make laws of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Section 185 of the Inland Revenue Act provides as follows:
Every person who sells or offers for sale, or who purchases any spirits, or has any spirits in his possession, knowing them to have been unlawfully manufactured or imported, shall, for first offence, incur a penalty not exceeding fifty dollars, and not less than ten dollars, and for each subsequent offence, a penalty of one hundred dollars; and all spirits so unlawfully manufactured or imported, wheresoever they are found, and all horses and vehicles and other appliances which have been or are being used for the purpose of removing the same, shall be forfeited to the Crown, and shall be dealt with accordingly.
It is considered necessary for the Inland Revenue Department . to have the entire control of all manufacture of spirits and this legislation not only increases the penalty against those who manufacture liquor illicitly, but with Tespect to those who try to sell it and are detected the fines are greatly increased.
Has that been the law heretofore?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes, it has been the law for years.

Mr. Speaker, before this
resolution carries I would ask to be per-

First let me say that at the Imperial Conference in London which I attended, in company with the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Robert Borden) and others of my colleagues in the Government, the ' question of naval policy, either for Canada or the Empire, was not discussed.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: To what year has the minister reference?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
1918. Certain negotiations, however, took place between the British Admiralty and the overseas representatives who were in London at the time. I myself, on certain occasions, discussed the naval defence of Canada with the First Sea Lord of the Admiralty, Sir Roslyn Wemyss, and also with the First Civil Lord, .Sir Eric Geddes. I also had the good fortune to have my right hon. friend the Prime Minister accompany me on one occasion when we reviewed the whole situation frankly and fairly. As a result of these conferences with the Admiralty a meeting of the Overseas Prime Ministers was held at the Savoy Hotel, London. Sir Robert Borden occupied the Chair at that meeting, and after a full discussion a memorandum was prepared, passed upon, and sent to the Admiralty, its date being 15th August, 1918. Before I read that memorandum I might be permitted to submit a letter accompanying it which was sent by Sir Robert Borden: Imperial Conference, 1918.
Decision of Dominions' Ministers re Navail Policy of Dominions.
Offices of the War Cabinet,
2 Whitehall Gardens, S.W. 1.
15th August, 1918.
Dear Sir Eric Geddes,-
I am afraid the brevity of the time at my disposal will prevent me bringing up in the Imperial War Cabinet the subject dealt with in the Admiralty memorandum.
I have, however, consulted the Prime Ministers of the Dominions, who (with the exception of the Prime Minister of Newfoundland), have expressed their approval of the accompanying memorandum.
The Prime Minister of Newfoundland has been requested to communicate with you direct on the subject.
Faithfully yours,
(Sd.) R. L. Borden.
The Right Honourable
Sir Eric Geddes, K.C.B., C.B.E., M.P.
The memorandum, which received the approval of all the Overseas Prime Ministers, with the exception of Dr. Lloyd, Premier of Newfoundland, reads as follows :
Memorahdum.
The Dominion Ministers, having considered the Admiralty Memorandum of May 17, 1918, on the Naval Defence of the British Empire, which was circulated to the Imperial War Conference, 1918, submit the following conclusions and observations.
1.	The proposals set forth in the Admiralty Memorandum for a single navy at all times under a central naval authority are not considered practicable.
2.	Purely from the standpoint of naval strategy the reasons thus put forward for the establishment of a single navy for the Empire under a central naval authority, are strong but not unanswerable. The experience gained in this war has shown that in time of war a Dominion Navy (e.g. that of Australia), can .operate with the highest efficiency as part of a united navy under one direction and command established after the outbreak of war.
3.	It is thoroughly recognized that the character of construction, armament andi equipment, and the methods and principles of training, administration and organization, should proceed upon the same lines in all the navies of the Empire. This policy has already been followed in those Dominions which have established naval forces.
4.	For this purpose the Dominions would welcome visits from a highly qualified representative of the Admiralty who, by reason of his ability and experience, would be thoroughly competent to advise the naval authorities of the Dominions in such matters.
5.	As naval forces come to be developed upon a considerable scale by the Dominions it may be necessary hereafter to consider the establishment for war purposes of some supreme naval authority upon which each of the Dominions would be adequately represented.
In consequence of the foregoing memorandum the Admiralty sent a highly technical and distinguished naval officer in the person of Admiral Viscount Jellicoe to visit the overseas Dominions.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: Before the minister proceeds, would it toe a breach of confidence on his part to tell us what the suggestion in the memorandum was to which the Prime Minister of Newfoundland refused to agree?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
I desire to make
it abundantly clear that the Prime Minister of Newfoundland did not refuse to agree to the suggestions contained in the memorandum. He did not happen to be present at the Conference between the overseas Prime Ministers, for what reason I am unable to state now, but I have no ground to suppose that the then Prime Minister of Newfoundland would have raised any dissenting voice to the memorandum I have just Tead.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: Has he agreed to it since?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
No. I was proceeding to say, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of this memorandum submitted on behalf

of Canada, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand, Admiral Viscount Jellicoe was instructed by the British Admiralty to visit the overseas Dominions, to consult with their governments, and to make reports to them as to what in his opinion would be the best policy for their adoption. Hon. members are quite familiar with the very lucid and useful suggestions offered to the Government of Canada by Lord Jellicoe whose report I tabled some weeks ago.
This Government carefully considered the suggestions contained in that report, but in view of the conditions which I mentioned to this House some weeks ago we decided to defer taking any action on them for the present. With the kind permission of hon. members I will again read to the House that memorandum in order that my remarks on Naval Affairs may appear in consecutive order in Hansard. This is the memorandum which I read on a previous occasion:
The Government has had under consideration for some time the question of the naval defence of Canada and the suggestion of Admiral Visoount Jellicoe in reference thereto.
In view of Canada's heavy financial commitments and of the fact that Great Britain has not as yet decided on her permanent naval policy, and of the approaching Imperial Conference at which the question of naval defence of the Empire will come up for discussion between the Home Government and the Overseas Dominions,	it has been	decided
to defer in the meantime action in regard to the adoption of a permanent naval policy for Canada.
The Government has decided to carry on the Canadian Naval	Service along	pre-war
lines and has accepted the offer of Great Britain of one light cruiser and two torpedo boat destroyers to take the place of the present obsolete and useless training ships, the Niobe and Rainbow.
The Minister of Naval Service, in order to be free to thoroughly reorganize and place the present service on an economical and efficient basis, has issued orders for the demobilization of all officers and naval ratings and for the discontinuance of civilian help at headquarters and at the Naval Dockyards in Esquimau and Halifax. The Canadian officers who are in the Imperial fleet and who are now being paid by the Canadian Government will be recalled and placed on duty with the Canadian Naval Service. The Naval College will also be continued. After reorganization has been completed, only those officers and other ratings and civilians will be taken on who are absolutely necessary and possess the qualifications desired.
I have nothing to add to that except to say that it is the Governments official statement on naval affairs at the present time.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
I did not hear exactly what my hon. friend said about the offer 
of some ships from the Mother Country to replace the Niobe and Rainbow. Has the Government accepted those ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
The Government
has not officially taken them over. Captain Hose, the Acting Director of Naval Service, is in England at the present time looking into the details, but the Government has officially notified the Admiralty that we do gratefully accept the offer of one modern light cruiser and two modern torpedo boat destroyers. I will have something more to say in regard to that offer as I proceed.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
Are any conditions attached to it?
Mr. DEPUTY' SPEAKER: Order. I must remind hon. members that the House is not in committee, and that therefore the minister should be allowed to place his remarks on Hansard in consecutive form without interruption.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
formed splendid service on the Pacific Coast. On instructions from the Admiralty she went to Mexico and brought safely to the port of Victoria the small British gunboats, the "Shearwater" and the "Algerine." While she did not meet any enemy ships, she was stripped for action and ready and anxious to meet them at any time, whatever the result might be. The "Niobe" was put in commission and steamed some 30,000 miles. On instructions from the Admiralty she and the "Rainbow" were finally taken out of active service. All their guns were removed in order that they might be placed on merchant vessels and both these ships were used from that time until the close of the war as depot ships. The Naval Service performed very excellent work also in providing patrols, especially on the Atlantic. In addition they maintained a regular mine-sweeping service on the trade routes and at entrances to har-hours, and on more than one occasion succeeded in sweeping out enemy mines.
A very active recruiting policy was carried on to get the necessary officers and men, as a result, 6,452 of all ranks were enrolled for the Canadian Naval Service, while 1,700 were enrolled in the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve (Overseas Division), and sent to England where they served in the Imperial Navy. This was done at the request of the Imperial Government. In addition, 82 wrere recruited for' the Royal Canadian Naval Air Service; 376 for the Imperial Motor Boat Patrol Service; 382 for the Royal Naval Air Force, a total of 8,992. The recruits were trained and placed in service with the greatest despatch consistent with efficiency. As fast as vessels could be procured and got ready they were put into commission.
The casualties suffered during the war totalled 26 officers and 158 men, including the 5 college graduates previously mentioned. One officer and 39 men of the Overseas Division of the Royal Canadian Naval ' Volunteer Reserve lost their lives. The Naval Service of Canada had to provide all the supplies necessary not only for their own ships but also for the ships of Great Britain and her allies operating in the vicinity of the Canadian coasts. The purchases *for stores alone amounted in 1917-18 to the large amount of $10,074,643. They also carried on at Halifax and. Esquimalt what was known as an examination service. This service was established shortly after the outbreak of war, all shipping on the re-

spective coasts being intercepted and examined before entering and leaving port.
I should like to say that the radiotelegraph service was found to be most efficient.
I should have failed in my duty if, before concluding my remarks regarding the Naval Service, I did not refer to the Naval Intelligence Department. While their work was secret, it was very necessary, and they performed their duties to the entire satisfaction, not only of the Naval Service of Canada, but of the Admiralty as well.
The total expenditure for naval purposes in the year 1918 amounted to the large sum of $33,367,433.09. The number of naval officers and ratings enrolled was 4,853, and the number of civilians employed was 1,375. The net cost, however, to the Canadian Government was only $11,527,727.48. The difference between the expenditures and the net cost represents the value of services rendered to the Imperial and Allied Governments, and illustrates forcibly the extent of that service.
As regards the Naval College, it might interest the House if I gave lust briefly the number of our young Canadians who have joined this service since the college started in 1911. One hundred and thirty-five joined all told, 68 of whom served in the Imperial service and 23 withdrew altogether. The number of Canadians now in the college is 45, and the Canadian Government have agreed that each year we shall send at the expense of Canada, eight of those cadets to be trained in the Imperial Navy, so that from time to time as occasion arises, when we require officers on our own ships, we shall be able to recall from the Imperial service those young Canadian officers who will have received a thorough training in the large fleet of the Home Government.
I might be permitted to refer to two of our young Canadian officers who have distinguished themselves in a signal manner in the Imperial Navy. I refer to Lieut. Brodeur, son of a former Minister of the Naval Service, who has been selected to specialize in gunnery and who at the present time is studying at the Royal Naval College at Greenwich. Besides him we have Lieut. Gauvreau, son of the hon. member for Temiscouata '(Mr. Gauvreau), who is presently serving in the Intelligence Branch at headquarters. Both of these very gallant and able young Canadian officers, as also the other young Canadian naval officers will be employed at headquarters or at Halifax.or on board the cruiser or destroyers. All of our Canadians who have served in the Imperial Navy have, I have been informed by the Admiralty, most excellent re-

cords. Therefore, the Government thought it the part of wisdom to continue to send, each year at the expense of the country, eight of our bright young graduates from the Naval College to receive training in the great home fleet and to be on call whenever the Canadian Government requires their services.
I should like to refer to the re-organization of the service. I have given the maximum number of officers, all ratings, and civilians employed in the Naval Service when the war was at its height. So that I might have a free hand to re-organize the entire Naval Service of Canada, with the consent of the Government I issued general demobilization orders to all naval ratings and to all civilians at headquarters, Esquimalt and Halifax, that their services would not be required on and after the 15th May. I did that so that I, as responsible head of the Naval Service, and my technical officers associated with me, might re-engage only those naval officers, ratings and civilians who possessed the necessary efficiency. Furthermore, my instructions were that only those who were absolutely needed and who possessed the requisite efficiency would be taken on. At the date those orders were issued we had, of naval ratings, 484, and of civilians, 819. Naval officers serving in the Imperial navy and officers and men at the college were not affected by those orders. The naval ratings consisted of 47 officers and 233 men attached to the Niobe at Halifax; 14 officers and 2 men attached to headquarters, and 23 officers, and 107 men attached to the Rainbow at Esquimalt. Of the civilian staff, 376 were employed at Halifax, 203 at headquarters and 240 at Esquimalt. This number has been reduced to 18 naval officers, 25 other ratings and 478 civilians. Therefore, the net reduction affected, both naval and civil, amounts to 782. In other words, I have reduced the personnel of naval officers and other ratings and civilians to the number of 521, as compared with the number of 1,303 naval officers and other ratings and civilians when demobilization orders were issued on March 25. The naval officers and civilians who are now in the employ of the Government are all men who possess the necessary knowledge and efficiency, and we certainly have not two men where only one is necessary.
I wish to refer to the generous gift of the Mother Country to Canada. I am sorry I cannot at the moment mention the name of the new cruiser that the British Government has been good enough to allocate to us, I expect in the course of a day or two
to get the name of that cruiser, but I have been informed by the Admiralty that she will be a modern cruiser, and her armament and speed will be as follows:
Displacement, 4,800 tons.
Length, 453 feet.
Breadth, 47 feet.
Draught, 16 feet, 8 inches.
Speed 25i knots.
Fuel capacity, 1,345 tons coal, 260 tons oil.
Armament, two 6-inch guns, ten 4-inch guns, four 3-pounder guns, four .303 Maxim, two .303 Maxim field guns, one 12-pounder field gun, two torpedo tubes
She will carry a full complement of approximately 20 officers and 384 men, or a total of 404.
The two modern destroyers that were built in 1916 are called the "Patriot" and "Patrician." They are vessels of 1,004 tons displacement:
Length, 271 feet.
Breadth, 27 feet, 6 inches.
Draught, 11 feet.
Speed, 35 knots.
Fuel capacity, 253 tons oil.
Armament, three 4-incli guns, one 2-inch pounder Pom Pom, four torpedo tubes.
They will carry full complements of 6 officers and 74 men, or a total of 80 each.
Some months ago the right hon. the Prime Minister accepted with thanks from the Admiralty the gift of two modem submarines known as H14 and H15. These vessels are of 364 and 434 tons displacement respectively. Their dimensions are as follows: Length, 150 ft. 3 in.; breadth, 15 ft. 9 in.; draught, 12 ft. 4 in; speed, 13 and 11 knots respectively; armanent, 4-18 in. bow tubes. They were built in 1918 and carry full complements of three officers and nineteen men, or a total of twenty-two. The total personnel of the two torpedo destroyers and the two submarines will amount to 608.
I think it might be in order for me to say here that although the Main Naval Estimates provide for an expenditure of only $300,000, the Supplementary Estimates will contain the further sum of $2,200,000, making a total expenditure for naval defence for the present fiscal year of $2,500,000. The reason that only $300,000 appears in the Main Estimates is that the Government were anxious to table the Estimates and our arrangements not being at that time completed with the Admiralty, we did not know just what we would be able to get from them in the way of ships. The House will bear in mind, then, when considering the Naval Estimates, that the total

ought to take measures to insure that her long coast lines and important seaports, as well as her Merchant marine should he amply protected at all times and against any eventuality.
With these few remarks I now ask that the House resolve itself into Committee of Supply to approve of the very modest expenditure of $2,500,000 for the Naval Expenditure for the year which we have entered upon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the hon. the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne) this afternoon is in such striking contrast to the statement made by him when he last addressed this House on the subject, that one finds it a little difficult to know just what the Government really has in mind in the announcement that has been made to-day. I am sure the people of this Dominion got the impression some months ago that the Government meant to do nothing by way of a naval policy until after the Imperial Conference which is to be held in London in 1921. Indeed, in his concluding remarks to-day the minister stated that it was the intention of the Government to do nothing in the way of adopting a permanent naval policy until after the Imperial Conference in 1921. But in the breath immediately preceding the minister told us that the Government had accepted from the British Government, one cruiser, two torpedo boat destroyers and two submarines, involving a personnel of 608 and requiring an outlay of $2,200,000 in addition to the amount which has been submitted in the Estimates for Naval Service. He speaks of this two millions as if it -were of no significance whatever. I find it difficult indeed to regard the acceptance of these ships, involving the personnel mentioned, and their maintenance, as other than an expression of naval policy. If it is not to be regarded as such, then I feel the minister should not come before the House and ask us to vote any money for this purpose.
The acceptance of these ships from the British Government means the adoption at the moment of a policy which is to be maintained, or it is a mere make-believe, for the period of the next year or two. At this, of all times, Parliament has the right to know all details of policy, either temporary or permanent, which the Government may have respecting naval matters.
I shall not attempt at the moment any criticism with respect to the acceptance of this gift beyond mentioning that on these matters Parliament should in

the first instance be consulted. The people of Canada have a right-through their representatives in this Parliament-to say whether or not at this time the country should be committed to an expenditure such as this afternoon the minister has announced we are to be asked to meet. We have this right as a Parliament, and the country should not have been committed to this course by secret negotiations made by the Prime Minister and 'his colleagues during the course of the last year, or the last few months. All that we have been told this afternoon is that negotiations 'have been carried on by the Prime Minister and his colleagues and some members of the British Admiralty. With this comes the announcement that certain commitments have been made by Order in Council in regard to none of which this Parliament has had the slightest intimation.
When the minister brought down 'his Estimates some little time ago they contained an item of $300,000, in connection with Naval Service, providing for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, and at that time he gave the country the impression that the intention of the Government was to reduce naval expenditures, and to reduce them to this very email amount. That impression has gone broadcast through, out the Dominion, and it has been accepted as the expressed view of the Government as to their policy for the present time. Today that whole position is completely reversed, and the minister now announces that in the Supplementary Estimates which are yet to be brought down, an additional expenditure t of o-ver $2,000,000 will be asked for. At the very beginning of the present session we, on this side, asked the Government to inform us, at as early a date as possible, of any matters of public significance which were likely to require the deliberation of Parliament. Certainly there are few questions of greater importance than this one of the Naval Service of the Dominion; and if the Government had intended a programme of this kind, Parliament was -entitled to have knowledge of it, not in the last fortnight of its siirigs but months ago so that there would have been opportunity to debate this question fully.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
The leader
of the Opposition will surely recall the fact that on March 24th I officially announced, in the name of the Government, that we were going to carry on the Naval Service of Canada along pre-war lines, and that is exactly what we are doing. The hon. member surely knows that we could not do

that on the sum of $300,000, and I have already explained -why that small sum is asked for.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
iLet me say
to the minister, first, that I fail to understand why he presented to Parliament the item which he di$ in the Main Estimates if he had something else in his mind. The only explanation that can b.e given is the one that we on this side have been repeatedly urging as t'he reason for the long delay of the Government in bringing down its Estimates: namely, that matters of great public significance may come to the attention of parliament only in the last few weeks of the session when a large amount of business has to be gotten through with in a great hurry. I think, Mr. Speaker, that a wave of indignation will sweep over this Dominion when the statement goes forth that, now that the war is over, at a time when we are considering in what way we can retrench on naval and military expenditures, and after the professions they have made, the Government have announced a programme involving an expenditure such as that which has been mentioned to-day, and more especially when the country learns that this has been done without Parliament having had any voice in the matter one way or the other. That, Mr. Speaker, is the exception I wish to take at the moment to the programme of the minister and of the Government. I shall, at the moment, say nothing as to whether it is right that Canada should or should not do this or that. I believe that Canada should assist in naval matters-in coast defence and co-operation in other ways-but I say that the country has a right to have its policy determined on the floor of Parliament and not in secret councils of the Cabinet. Certainly in this matter, the Government have shown a complete indifference to the rights of the people, through their representatives in this House, in giving no opportunity whatever for the country to say whether or not these ships shall be accepted, whether or not the expenditures they will involve shall be incurred, whether or not we are to launch upon such a programme at the present time. All that the Government have said is that they have no policy, and will have no policy, until after the Imperial Conference in 1921.
I shall wait until we get into committee to speak further on this subject. At the moment I wish simply to voice what I believe to be the sentiment of public indignation which will be everywhere felt throughout the Dominion when it is learned
that the Government have committed this country, in the matter of naval expenditures, to a programme which they have led the country to believe would not be undertaken at this time, and have placed Parliament in the position of being obliged either to refuse to accept ships which the Government have already accepted-and as the minister has said gratefully thanked the Imperial Government for-or else to undertake a commitment which is only the beginning of the spending of many millions on matters pertaining to naval defence.
Motion agreed to and the House went into Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Naval- Service-To provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy, $300,0-00.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: Let me ask the minister this question. He has figured that in the Supplementary Estimates, he would request from Parliament a vote of $2,200,000 in .addition to the $300,000 to provide for the maintenance of the Royal Canadian Navy? The minister of course expects Parliament to vote all the additional amounts that are set forth in t'he Estimates on page 47 in regard to Naval Service, such as hydrographic survey, fisheries protection service, a radiotelegraph service, and the other branches that are mentioned as part of the Naval Service. That is correct, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: I may explain, Mr. Chairman, that this afternoon I was speaking of what should be termed strictly naval expenditures. In addition to the $300,000 mentioned here, there will be a sum of $2,200,000 in the Supplementary Estimates. The Fisheries Branch was, some years ago, under the regime of my predecessor, transferred from the Marine Department to the Naval Service. I am now transferring the Fisheries Branch from the Naval Service back to the Marine Department, and that will take effect on the 1st July next. I am also transferring back to the Marine Department the control of the life-saving stations. . I think that when hon. members are considering the naval expenditure of Canada they ought to consider only this $300,000, and the $2,200,000 which will appear in the Supplementary Estimates, because these other items have really nothing to do with the question o,f our naval force. Even if Gandda did not have a Naval Service, provision would still have to be made for hydrographic survey work, fisheries protection, etc.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext: These additional expenditures come to about. $1,365,000. Adding the amount the minister has mentioned as being required for the Naval Service would bring the total expenditure under this division close to the $4,000,000 mark.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
What is the
reason for all these items being put in under the head of Naval Service? Have members of the Naval Service nothing whatever to do with these other branches?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
As I explained a
moment ago, my predecessor, Sir Douglas Hazen, transferred the fisheries' protection service and these other items to the Naval Service. It was felt at the time there was not sufficient work to keep busy those engaged in the Naval Service Department, hence the transfer. I intend now to transfer those branches back to where they more properly belong,-the Marine Department; as the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) suggested some time ago. But the actual naval expenditure, I repeat once more, is only $2,500,000.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY HON. C. C. BALLANTYNE, MINISTER OF NAVAL AFFAIRS.
speechtext:
So the country is now
asked to entirely ignore the announcement which the minister made in the month of March that our naval expenditure would be considerably reduced during the coming year. This announcement, as he himself knows, was received with gratification from one end of the country to the other. During the previous year about $600,000 was expended on the Naval Service proper, and we were told that only $300,000 was to be expended for the current year; and in order to make his announcement still more emphatic the minister declared that he had ordered the

demobilization of the officers and men engaged in our Naval Service. Now we find that not only is there no reduction in the naval expenditure, but, on the contrary, it is to be increased to $2,250,000. And yet no naval policy has so far been announced! Last March in the statement he very carefully made to the House* the hon. minister declared that no naval expenditure would be entered upon until after the Imperial Conference. He did not at that time expect that the Conference would take place before 1921. But now we are confronted with an entirely different official declaration. It is not $300,000 that we are asked to spend on the Naval Service this year, but $2,500,000. And, remember, Mr. Chairman, this is not for any new naval policy at all, it is only an avant-gout of what is going to happen. If $2,500,000 is going to be spent when no naval policy' has been adopted, and when no Imperial Conference has been held, what amount will the minister ask for when the great official Imperial Naval Policy is launched? Then we may have a yearly expenditure of $15,000,000 or $20,000,000.
I said a minute ago that the statement of the minister regarding a reduction in our naval expenditure was received throughout the length and breadth of the country with gratification. Why? Because we are facing the most serious financial exigency in the history of this country. Our national debt is tremendous, and its liquidation is calling upon the people for greater and greater efforts. We are overwhelmed with new taxation of all kinds. Yet at the very time when this burdensome taxation is imposed upon our shoulders, suddenly, in fiat contradiction of what was proclaimed in this House in March, we are asked to spend $2,250,000 on the Naval Service. 1 wish to record my protest against this expenditure. I say that the Government should at least have waited until it had a definite naval policy to place before the country. We remember what happened in 1911. The new government of that day, presided over by the same right hon. gentleman -who is the head of this Government, said: "We will not develop the naval policy of our predecessors in office." The country was with him at that time, everything was stopped. Since 1911 events of tremendous world importance have taken place and the countries of Europe are to-day overburdened with war debts. In these circumstances we were under the impression that we had ample time to develop a naval policy, and we did not expect to embark upon any new naval expenditure. I cannot agree

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: with the minister in his present action. Let him wait until the Conference has been held, let us see what policy will be proposed, let us get rid of some of this heavy debt that is bearing down upon us, and then we will decide what should be done in regard to naval defence in the interests of Canada and of the Empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My good friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) is as a rule very lucid in his argument, but to-day I do not find him so. On March 25 I made it as clear as I possibly could that the Government had decided not to adopt any permanent naval policy, but to wait the outcome of the Imperial Conference and a declaration by Great Britain on Imperial Naval Policy, and our heavy financial commitments also exerted a strong influence on our decision. I also made it clear that the Government was going to continue the Naval Service along pre-war lines. Listening to my hon. friend, one would think that Canada had never spent more than $600,000 on the Naval Service, but even in 1911-12 I find that the expenditure was $1,790,017.16. If this Government had not done anything whatever but' simply allow the obsolete service to continue, I would now be before the House asking for an expenditure of $2,322,207. Now, for a much improved and much more efficient service we are asking for $2,500,000. From the remarks he has made I take it that my hon. friend (Mr. Boland) is in favour of abolishing the Naval Service; of providing no expenditure whatever for it. We are merely carrying along the service od pre-war lines; we are really not increasing the naval expenditure by one dollar. The Estimate now before us is for an amount less than the cost of maintaining the Canadian Naval Service of pre-war times, having due regard to the differences in wages, the increased cost of provisions, coal, and everything else. Moreover, we are providing for modem ships, efficient in every way. I do not wish to enter into any political controversy with regard- to naval matters, but we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that in pre-war times wTe were spending over $1,000,000 a year on the Naval Service, and if we were doing nothing more to-day than what we did then we would be spending $2,322,207 on a service that would be almost entirely useless. What good was the Niobe? What good was the Rainbow? We were spending $450,000 a year in keeping the Niobe tied up at the dock at Halifax-

Whose fault was that?
Mr. BALLANTYNr,: Will the hon. gentleman allow me? We were spending $250,000 a year to keep the Rainbow tied up.

The Rainbow is a good
boat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will have ample opportunity later to explain his technical knowledge of naval affairs.
I do not want to be disagreeable to the minister, but he himself made it plain to the House a moment ago that both the Niobe and the Rainbow rendered splendid service during the war. '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will not withdraw anything I said about the good service rendered by the Niobe and the Rainbow during the war. But I repeat that they are both obsolete vessels. I find no fault 'with any Government in that regard, but hon. members will agree that ships 'built in 1891 are not modern ships. Both these ships are now in such condition that we could not possibly put them into commission. My hon. friend (Mr. Duff) shakes his head, but I am stating the facts. In view .of the fact that the Government are providing for a more efficient service at not a dollar of increased expenditure over that of pre-war times, I am satisfied that hon. members and the people generally will approve of the Government's policy. But I do not want a wrong impression to prevail. The Auditor General's report may show that $600,000 was spent on the navy for one year, but it must be remembered that the balance of the heavy expenditure that was entailed was charged to demobilization. In 1911, 1912 and 1913 we spent on the Naval Service of Canada more than $1,000,000 a year, and I repeat that having regard to the increased cost of everything we are really make a less expenditure when we ask for $2,500,000 this year.

How many officers and men will be in the Naval Service of Canada when the light cruiser, two destroyers and two submarines come into the hands of the Canadian Government? Will more men be employed in the Naval Service than were employed before? I ask the question because I fear that quite involuntarily the minister is leading the country into error when he claims that he will carry the service now outlined for $2,500,000 a year. My impression is that when the year is over and we meet in the next session-if there is no election before that-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There won't be.
Don't be cocksure.

-the minister will have a large amount of Supplementary Estimates to place before the House. I understand that only the senior officer on the light cruiser is to be obtained from the Old Country; that all the other officers and men will be Canadians and in the pay of the Canadian Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: Is that a larger number than the number who previously served in our naval forces?

I do not agree that the announcement made in March with regard to proposed changes effecting a reduction of our naval services was received with satisfaction by the country. It may have been received with satisfaction by those surrounding the hon. member (Mr. Beland), or in his portion of the Dominion, but my impression is that throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion the feeling was distinctly the opposite. The statement that we were not to take our part as a nation; that we were not to support other nations of like mind to ourselves, was received not only with .concern .but with feelings akin to shame by the people. The country has been educated to the idea that Canada should support her own navy. It is not many years since the hon. gentleman's leader, .and at that time my leader, submitted an eloquent argument, backed by many figures and estimates, that we should have a navy of our own. In fact, he actually let contracts for the construction of fast cruisers of the Bristol type, which would have cost much more than the proposals now put forward. The country experienced a feeling of pride that at last Canada was to do her part instead of depending upon another part of the Empire to defend her coasts. But the ^expenditure now proposed is not to be compared with that recommended by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Well, the people got into that frame of mind, and that frame of mind is not to ;be easily changed simply because of the political exigency of a party being in opposition rather than in office. The majority of the people insist upon our adopting a self-respecting naval policy. Here we have a proposal to accept -
from the British Government a cruiser, two destroyers and two submarines, thus keeping alive, until a permanent naval policy for the Dominion can be decided upon, that Naval Service which we should maintain as one of the nations of the British Empire. This will keep in the service those men who are now in the service and who are in those vessels which did excellent service during the war, but which are now undoubtedly obsolete and should be scrapped; whereas if this estimate were to be defeated and the money were not appropriated, those men would all have to be demobilized; they would go into other occupations; they would be lost to the service, and Canada would lose a very great asset. This is merely continuing the policy that we have always had; but instead of having obsolete ships of which we are not at all proud, no matter what good work they did during the war, we shall, with this new service, have modern, up-to-date, efficient ships, on which our men may get training and become better sailors and gunners than any we have had before.
I rise not for the purpose of' discussing the matter in detail, but of protesting against the proposition to whittle away Estimates for a Canadian Navy. Canada is as a whole prepared, not to agree to a proposition of this kind, but to go on and do her part in keeping up the proper defence work of Canada on the high seas, thus preserving her self-respect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) referred to what he terms a feeling of shame that swept over the country after the announcement made by the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne) in March last. If there was a feeling of shame, it was that the Government announced at that time that it had no naval policy -whatever, and the country was ashamed of having in power a Government that had no policy on such an important branch of the public administration. When the hon. member contrasted the situation as it was in 1311 with the situation as it is to-' day, he left out of account altogether the one material factor. In 1311 a grave menace through the existence of the German navy faced the world. Lord Jellicoe, who was retained by the Government to report on the naval situation, presented a report, and on page 6 of that report, which I hold in my hand and which has been presented to Parliament, he says:	" The German
menace has now disappeared." The condition as regards naval defence is therefore to-day entirely different from what it was in 1911. The whole situation, from the point

of view both of danger to countries from attack at sea, and the ability of countries to cope with the vast military and naval expenditures, is entirely the opposite of what it was at the time the naval policy was launched. If there be one thing above another that is apparent from what the minister said this afternoon, it. is that the Government was very much to blame after assuming office in 1911 in failing to carry on and carry out the ipolicy inaugurated by the Laurier Administration. When war broke out, if instead of the Niobe and the Rainbow, we had had a fleet on the Atlantic and on the Pacific as was planned under that policy, and as would have been in existence had that policy been carried out, it is difficult to say. what splendid part Canada might not have played on the sea as well as on land in the great war. The minister has given us to-day sufficient evidence to prove that even with the two vessels which were established under the Laurier naval policy, and which would not have been in existence but for that policy, Canada was able to render at sea very material service at a critical time.
The point we are taking exception to this afternoon is not that Canada should do something by way of naval defence. Our criticism is directed against the change of attitude on the part of the Ministry in regard to what Canada should do, and when she should do it. In March last, the minister announced clearly that, owing to the fact that there was to be an Imperial Conference in 1921, it was not desirable to incur large expenditures for naval defence at this time, and concurrently with that announcement by the minister came the Estimates to Parliament indicating a reduction in expenditure from $600,000 to $300,000. The Opposition did not make those reductions. If the amounts do not represent all that the Government expended or intended to expend in the past on naval matters, that is the fault of the minister or his department in drawing up those Estimates. But the inference the country got at that time was that the Government intended to retrench in naval as well as in other matters. Let me read the statement made by the minister on the 25th March, which constitutes the only announcement given out by him. At page 737 of Hansard, the minister is reported as saying:
Before the Orders of the Day are called I desire to make a statement on the Government's policy in regard to naval affairs :
The Government has had under consideration for some time the question of the naval defence of Canada and the suggestion of Admiral Viscount Jellieoe in reference thereto.
In view of Canada's heavy financial commitments and of the fact that great Britain has not as yet decided on her permanent naval policy and of the approaching Imperial Conference at which the question of naval defence of the Empire will come up for discussion between the Home Government and the Overseas Dominions, it has been decided to defer in the meantime action in regard to the adoption of a permanent naval policy for Canada.
If that paragraph carries any impression with it-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Read on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will do so in a moment. If that paragraph carries any impression with it-and it is the outstanding paragraph in the minister's announcement-it is that Canada has heavy financial *commitments at the present time; that Great Britain has no permanent naval policy; that next year there is to be a conference at which a policy will be decided upon, and that in the meantime the Government will defer adoption of any permanent policy in Canada. I contend that the acceptance of a cruiser, two torpedo boat destroyers and two submarines is evidence of a policy. The minister cannot say that no policy is . involved in the acceptance of those ships, which will mean the support of a complement of 600 or 700 men, in addition to all that is required in equipment and administration. If the Ministry have a policy for a Canadian Naval Service, let them state it to Parliament and let us act accordingly; but the minister says: "We have no policy at the present time; we are going to have a policy in 1921." What we say is:	"The situation financially being
what it is in the world to-day and the danger as regards attacks at sea being what it is, we can well afford during the period of one year to keep the figures of naval expenditure at the estimate at which the minister has indicated they would be kept.
The minister asked me to read the balance of his statement. It is as follow?
The Government has decided to carry on the Canadian Naval Service along pre-war lines and has accepted the offer of Great Britain of one light cruiser and two torpedo boat destroyers to take the place of the present obsolete and useless training ships, the Niobe and Rainbow.
The disposition there is on pre-war lines. In other words, the Rainbow and Niobe were used simply as training ships to train a few men without involving very great expenditure or a very large personnel. Can the minister tell me what the personnel on those two ships was before the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had 784 naval ranks and ratings and 321 civilians, or 1,105



all told. I should like to draw the hon. gentleman's atention to the fact that with this improved service we purpose having only 608 naval ratings and 478 civilians.
About the same number.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask whether in addition to the personnel of these ships, the staffs that will be required for the Naval colleges and the like will add considerably in numbers to the appointments to the Naval Servcie?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have in the Naval College 12 officers and 46 men, a total of 58.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Had the minister in mind, at the time he made this statement, the addition of this cruiser, the two torpedo boat destroyers, and the two submarines, and their maintenance with this personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I certainly had in mind and the 'Government certainly had in mind a complete reorganization of the Naval 'Service, but we had not at that time completed our arrangements as we have announced them to-day. I had informed the Government that it was absolutely necessary to reorganize our Naval Service which was in a most inefficient state.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What I wanted to know was whether the minister and the Government had in mind, as an outcome of that reorganization, that during the present year this cruiser and the two torpedo -boat destroyers and the two .submarines would become a part of the Canadian Naval Service and would have to be maintained as such?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will refeT to Admiral Jellicoe's report he will see that the minimum scheme placed before the Government involved an expenditure of $10,000,000 extending over a number of years up, I think, to 1925 or 1927.
