Admiral Jellicoe states in that report that the ships will be a gift to the Canadian Government. Inasmuch as the Government could not see its way clear to incur such heavy expenditure, we had to re-open negotiations with the Admiralty to see if we could get the one cruiser and the two destroyers, and when I made my announcement on Alarch 25 those negotiations had not been completed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That must be incorrect because in his announcement the minister says that the cruiser and the tor-
[Mr. Ballantyne.I
pedo boat destroyers have been accepted. Here are his words:
The Government has accepted the offer of Great Britain of one light cruiser and two torpedo boat destroyers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We had at that moment actually accepted the offer but we had not received word from the Admiralty that we were going to get the ships.
Surely they would keep their word.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister could hardly accept a gift that had not been made. The Government must have had the gift made to it before it could accept it. The point I am somewhat concerned about at the moment is that if the ministry had in contemplation this naval unit or. whatever one may choose to call it, why was it that in the Estimates subsequently submitted, an appropriation was not presented to Parliament for this larger expenditure? Can the minister answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot add anything to what I have stated in my remarks this afternoon. On Alarch 25 we did not know what the actual expenditure was going to be. It is true that the Government had accepted the ships, but we had not heard from the Admiralty. The Admiralty, through Admiral Jellicoe, offered us certain ships providing we adopted a programme that would cost this country annually not less than $10,000,000. We did not see our way to embarking on such an expenditure, and we said that we were prepared to take one cruiser and two destroyers but at that date we did not know that that would be agreeable to the Admiralty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister announced this afternoon that the Prime Minister himself had accepted the two submarines previously. Why was no mention made of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is easily explained. The two submarines had been accepted quite a number of months previously. When the Prime Minister was in England these two submarines were lying at Bermuda, and they were offered to Canada, the offer being made personally to the Prime Minister when he was in London, and they were accepted by him. I will find out the exact date, but I should imagine it was six or eight months before we accepted the cruisers and the destroyers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If they had already been accepted by the Prime Minister, why did not the minister mention them in making his statement to the House. To-day is the first time the country has been informed that these two submarines had been accepted, in addition to these two torpedo boat destroyers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think it must be clear to every one and to the leader of the Opposition that when I made the statement that the Government were going to carry on on pre-war lines, it meant that we were going to ask for the same expenditure that had been asked for in pre-war years. Nothing could be clearer than that. I certainly did not mislead the House in any way. If I had not stated 'that the Government were going to carry on along pre-war lines, my hon. friend might have been justified in coming to the conclusion he apparenly has come to, tout when I stated that we would carry along on prewar lines, it meant that the expenditure would be the same as in pre-war years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We had no cruiser in pre-war times, and we had no submarines or torpedo boat destroyers. We had a couple of training ships. The minister completely evades my question as -to why he did not announce to the House on March 25 that the Prime Minister had accepted these two ships. It seems to me an extraordinary thing that the Prime Minister, notwithstanding the great powers that he has as Prime Minister, should feel free .to accept a couple of submarines on behalf of this country without conferring with his colleagues in the Ministry in regard to such an acceptance. I think that is an exercise of power that is scarcely warranted. In the same way I think the acceptance of a cruiser and a couple of torpedo boat destroyers, in addition to these two submarines, without ever asking Parliament whether such a gift should be accepted, is going very far beyond what the Governor in Council or the Prime Minister and his colleagues should have gone in a matter which commits the country to such vast expenditures.
To conclude the minister's statement on the Naval policy, he went on:
The Minister of Naval Service, in order to be free to thoroughly reorganize and place the present service on an economical and efficient basis, has issued orders for the demobilization of all officers and naval ratings and for the discontinuance of civilian help at headquarters and at the Naval Dockyards in Esquimau and Halifax. The Canadian officers who are in the Imperial fleet and who are now being paid by the 223J
Canadian Government wilf be recalled and placed on duty with the Canadian Naval Service. The Naval College will also he continued. After reorganization has been completed, only those officers and other ratings and civilians will be taken on who are absolutely necessary and possess the qualifications desired.
I submiit that any person reading that statement and without having any knowledge of what had been secretly arranged by the minister in advance would get the impression that the Government intended beween that time and the time the permanent policy was decided upon to get along on as 6mall an expenditure as possible, reducing the personnel to as small a margin as possible, and that before anything in the nature of a permanent policy was adopted Parliament would be informed of what the Government's intentions were. That., I submit, is the lea^t that was owing to Parliament and ,to the people of Canada.
I do not think we should he asked at this time-in view of the attitude which the country has been led to. believe would govern the situation,-I do not think we should be asked on a few minutes' notice to vote $2,000,000 over and above anything " that is already dn the main Estimates, and for something that is over and above anything so far suggested in regard to the Naval Service.

I stand by the Laurier naval policy and I congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of Marine for having in spite of the bad company surrounding him remained faithful to that policy. I have noticed that his policy, which was Sir Wilfrid Lauriers was supported this afternoon only by one Liberal Unionist, and he the gentleman representing the seamen of Park-dale (Mr. Mowat). I did not notice that there was any particular enthusiasm display by the old crew-the old Tory party which in 1911 and since combatted so vehemently the "Laurier disloyal policy," as they called it, and which is now presented to the country by the Minister of the Naval Affairs in the Unionist Government, as the salvation of Canada and of the British Empire.
I stand by the Laurier naval policy in normal times. In 1911 I defended it, I risked my political life in its support, but the Liberal party was defeated on that policy through the alliance of a jingo party with the Nationalist party. I abide by the verdict of the Canadian people. We were informed by the old Government, that a new policy would be launched and that it would be submitted to the people. Mr. Chairman, we know what happened. In 1913 the Premier came before Parliament with a new

naval programme consisting of a proposed gift to the Admiralty of three dreadnaughts. By the way, dreadnaughts are quite discarded to-day. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right in 1913 when he told the Government that the best naval experts of Great Britain were opposed to the construction of these dreadnaughts. But, let that pass and let us come to the point.
I said a moment ago that I stood by the Naval Act of 1910, which was defeated at the polls in 1911, that in 1913 a new policy was propounded but nothing came of it because the Senate of Canada, led at the time by the ex-Prime Minister of Ontario, iSir George Ross, brought the Government to its senses, reminding them that there was on the statute book a Naval Act which had not yet been repealed. The war came along, and now that it is over, when Canada is facing financial liabilities to the amount of nearly three billion dollars, the conditions are not normal and whilst I was in favour of the Laurier policy which was defeated at the polls in 1911, I am perfectly logical [DOT]* in stating that I cannot stand for it to-day, in view of the heavy financial commitments of the country. The amount is not very large-$2,700,000-and even if it were larger, I have enough confidence in the business sense, and honesty of purpose of the minister to say that under qrdinary circumstances I would leave to him the free expenditure of that money. But $2,700,000 for naval expenditures is not needed to-day after the victory which was achieved by the Allies on the sea as well as on the land in 1918. That $2,700,000 with $5,000,000, which we voted the other evening for the Royal Mounted Police, -which is not needed in central Canada, and for militia, makes nearly $8,000,000. $8,000,000 might go far towards paying the widows and orphans of our gallant soldiers who died at the front, and towards defraying the Pension Bill. I call the attention of ,my fellow members who know what the hardships of the people are, to the fact that the only policy with the people of Canada to-day is one of, retrenchment. Where can that retrenchment be made if not in the Militia and Naval Service Departments?
We have no fear to-day. If there was one fact which was pre-eminent in the war it was the superiority of the British Navy. And if ever there was a black Friday for our enemy, Germany, it was when she surrendered her navy to the British Fleet in the midst of the ocean. The German navy was ignominiously wiped out. Therefore, where is the enemy on the seas to be

faced by the British Navy? A moment ago my hon. friend, quoting the words of the Rt. Hon. Walter Long, said that the only country in the world which could pretend to be a rival of Great Britain in so far as a navy is concerned was the American Republic. Does any one in this House seriously believe that we shall have in the future to fear the enmity of the United States? Sir, every statesman of Great Britain has declared over and over again in the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge, that in their computations of expenditure of the British Navy they have always put aside the contingency of war with the United States of America. There is to-day, an spite of the usual election lion tail-twisting, a real, a true, a sincere friendship, between the AnglonSaxon peoples both of the United States and of the Mother Couptry. There is no peril, there is no danger, there is no necessity to-day for even the expenditure mentioned by my hon. friend. On the contrary there is an urgent necessity to cut dawn expenditure in order to put Canada on her feet again because she is burdened with such financial commitments that it would take her many long years before she can compete successfully with the other nations of the world. Besides Mr. Chairman, we have manfully done our share for the Mother Country, and we should not come Vith this picayune tribute of $2,200,000 a year to the British Exchequer. My hon. friend a moment ago spoke of a patrol on the Pacific Ocean.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Atlantic ocean.

Yes, and my hon. friend mentioned the Pacific ocean, too. He knows that on the Atlantic ocean we have nothing to fear. With respect to the Pacific ocean the treaty with Japan is about to ibe renewed; and I understand that to Australia has been assigned by the Mother Country the duty of patrolling a certain zone in that ocean. At all events, Mr. Chairman, the treaty with Japan is to he renewed very shortly, and we have no reason to entertain fear on that score. The minister said that he meant to administer this Naval Act according to -the principles of local autonomy which are embodied in it. I am afraid, from a certain remark which he let slip, during his speech this afternoon, that the true Canadian spirit has not yet penetrated his mind! ;cam(pletely. Jf he -means to administer this Act according to Canadian views, and Canadian ideals- not rejecting at all the idea of co-operation with the Mother Country in case of emergency, because the Naval Act of 1910 speci-

fies that-my hon. friend has paid his respects to the Navy League of Canada. Well, I know the gentlemen who are the sponsors of the various branches of the Navy League in Canada. They are respectable and well meaning gentlemen hut they are not the friends olf Canadian autonomy- they are not Canadians, first, last and always. From the circular letter which I received the other day, from Mr. Aeanilius Jarvis, President of the Navy League in Toronto, that gentleman does not dream of a .Canadian Navy. He dreams olf a tribute for the Imperial Navy paid for by Canada. That is what he dreams of; and when my hon. friend pays such compliments to the Navy League, I am afraid that the Laurier navy may be used by him as a weapon which might serve the Imperialist cause.
Mr. Chairman, has my hon. friend thought very seriously of what he is doing this afternoon? He has laid down a policy which was denounced by one whom he should respect-whom all of us in this House should respect-as being "absurd, unworkable, dangerous and revolutionary."
Who said that?

My hon. friend is propounding a naval policy which As "absurd, unworkable, dangerous and revolutionary." Now, whoever uttered those words? My hon. friend may say, " I belong to a different Government. This is a Unionist Government, and I am not responsible for the old Tory Government. I am a Unionist minister, and therefore I represent only Unionist principles." But my hon. friend cannot disassociate himself from the right hon. gentleman to whom I refer, whether the latter is Prime Minister in a Unionist Cabinet or was Prime Minister in a Tory Cabinet. It is the same Sir Robert Laird Borden to whom I have reference-it is the same individual, and the same personality, and we cannot allow him to change his mind as it pleases him to change it on such a vital issue. Now, in 1911 when this policy -which is adopted by my hon. friend as the policy of the Unionist Government- was presented to the country by the late lamented (Sir Wilfrid Laurier, it was denounced by the present Prime Minister-then the leader of the Opposition-as being " absurd, unworkable, dangerous and revolutionary." Well, Sir, I am surprised to see such a peaceful, law-abiding citizen-
Such a Christian.

-as my hon. friend the Minister of Marine-who did his share in
the great war for the Empire and the Mother Country-I am surprised that he should come before the House and forward a policy which was denounced by his present leader as being, " absurd, unworkable, dangerous and revolutionary." Surely he will have to explain the process -by which he has been able to alter the views of the right hon. gentleman. And besides, X might recall to my hon. friend the fact-that his leader olf to-day solemnly stated in years gone by that no naval policy of' any kind-least of all the Laurier naval policy which my hon. friend accepts today-should go into force without first-being submitted to the people of Canada-Now, Sir, on February 3, 1910, on the motion for the third reading of the Bill which is now the Naval Act, Sir Robert Borden, then Mr. R. L. Borden, said:
I am as strong as any man in this country in the belief that it is the duty of Canada to participate upon a permanent basis in the defence of this Empire and to do our reasonable share in that regard, hut X say that to attempt to force a policy of this kind upon the people of this country without giving them an opportunity to say yea or nay with regard to it would be one of the worst mistakes that could be made by any man really favoured that policy.
Mr. Chairman, as I stated a moment ago, that very policy was defeated at the polls in 1911. Our Canadian Navy was frowned down by the albpowerful Tories of 1911, 1912, 1913 and 1914. Then it was suddenly taken up as, after all, the best means of protection for our sea-coast during the war, and it accomplished something. As evidence of that we have had the very words of my hon. friend this afternoon. Now, it has been found so adaptable to Canada that my hon. friend presents it as being the policy of the Government.
But what regard has the Government for the sacred rights of the people? What does my hon. friend from Perth whom I see before me just now, think of his Tory Government accepting the policy which he denounced with such vehemence during the campaign of 1911? Then the Simon-pure Tory candidates promised that no Buch policy would ever be adopted by Parliament unless the people of Canada were consulted. Well, the people have never been consulted, and we have this show-because it is nothing else hut a show-where can be seen the various ministers of 1911, 1912 and 1913, making the somersaults I have been describing.
I expect to hear from my stern unbending Tory friends on this question. Were they sincere in 1911 when they denounced the

Laurier naval policy as being un-British and disloyal, and as being the first step towards separation from the Mother Country? Were the leaders of the Tory party sincere? They have since joined hands with the Liberal-Unionists, and it seems to me that the latter are "putting one over" their Tory friends to-day. Listen to the hon. Minister of Naval Service, who is so proud to carry out the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Listen to the echo, from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) saying, "Amen; that is my policy, that is the policy I defended in 1911." But what are the real Tories thinking, what are they saying? 1 want to hear from them to know if they were in earnest in 1911?

I do not think I ever heard a speaker who so thoroughly answered and confuted himself as the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Lemieux) He has completely boxed the compass and taken up every phase of the question, always returning to the fact that this is a continuance of the Laurier policy, which he now condemns. This policy, which he insists is a continuation of the Laurier policy, he objects to being continued on the ground of retrenchment. He therefore disowns his own child and ignores his own relatives-and I do not blame him. In the past we said: "That is exactly what the Laurier policy will lead to"; we said it would lead to a continuance and an expansion of expense and pretention, which was absurd and would be ineffective. And we are now "up against it." I do not think that any one will deny that, if it were not for the exigencies of the situation, there would be the least excuse for going on with such an Estimate as this-not the slightest. During that long-distance naval debate we insisted that the Empire was an empire, our object being to show that we should not have a series of fleets, but one great Empire fleet, and that we would assume whatever our portion of the cost of that fleet was adjudged to be and build and develop it accordingly. The Laurier policy, founded upon the Naval Service Act, pre-supposed that we were not in the Empire at all, that when We said we were in the Empire we would be in it, but in the meantime we were out of it, and that it would be better for us to go on and build our own fleet with complete equipment from beginning to end. Then-as we predicted-when a heavy burden like the present would come upon us we would have this absurd display to keep up, or else we would fall into disgrace and contempt. It is possible at the present

time to annihilate this Estimate. How? By annihilating the, idea o,f the Laurier fleet. That is what you are pleading for, and yet you call us inconsistent. We are simply saying that we are marking time, waiting for the development of a naval policy which will be declared next year. And if I thought the Government at the present time were asking for this expenditure with any other idea than marking time, I would vote against it. But I know they are only marking time in order that later we may develop a proper Imperial nav.al policy.
The Laurier naval policy, if it had been carried out, and if we were in power now- as we are-would demand not $2,700,000, but more likely $20,700,000. The people of this country are grateful to the old Tory party, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) has said, for preserving them from an absurdity that can only be likened to the well-known fable of the frog which, being determined to blow itself to the size of the bull, blew itself up altogether.

The Minister of Naval
Affairs this afternoon made a very important statement on naval matters. Like myself, he does not know anything about the technical side of naval affairs, and I would not have referred to his ignorance except for the fact that he taunted ime a few minutes ago with my absolute lack of knowledge of naval technique. But I think, Sir, that I can perhaps deal with the situation in Canada in respect to naval matters as well as the Minister of Naval Affairs, and if I may be permitted I would like for a few minutes to discuss this very important question.
I want to say, first, that I think it is due to this House that after the minister made this very important statement on naval affairs he should have moved that the committee report progress on this item of the Estimates so as to give hon. members a chance to study his statement. I am waiting to see if the minister will do so now. As he has not seen fit to accept my suggestion, I presume I will have to go on.
There is bound to be a difference of opinion in this country as to whether or not a naval policy should be adopted by Canada. We heard the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) say that when Parliament and the people were told in March that the Government did not propose to go on with a naval policy there was a feeling of relief all over the country; and we also heard the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) dispute

that statement and say that the people wanted a naval policy. While perhaps in that part of the country from which the hon. member for Parkdale comes that sentiment may prevail, yet I assert-and I say it with all modesty-that perhaps there is no hon. gentleman who in the past 18 months has received so much correspondence in regard to naval matters as I have; and there is perhaps very good reason for that being the case. Prom every part of this country,

from Toronto- and other cities; from most of the important towns of Canada; from the Pacific coast; from the Atlantic coast; from clergymen, lawyers, doctors and every other class of citizens, I have received letters with regard to -the Canadian Navy, expressing the view that it would not 'be good business, that it would not be dn the interests of the country, to- spend one dollar on Naval Services 'at the present time. I -do not wish to occupy unduly the time of the -committee in this connection, -but perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Mowat) will listen to something which comes from his own city-Toronto. Here is what the Toronto Saturday Night says:
Sir Robert Borden has started on what may be termed a world tour with Admiral Viscount Jellicoe, which has been subjected to interruption, but no doubt it was intended to enter into discussions from which some plan would be forthcoming with suggestions that Australia, South Africa and Canada participate. What plans the Admiral has in mind is, of course, yet unknown, but it all brings up the question as to whether or not any satisfactory plans as regards a definite naval programme could be devised at this time.
First of all, if this League of Nations is worth a whoop, which a good many of us are now inclined to doubt, navies of any size will be unnecessary. But more important is the fact that authorities cannot agree among themselves as to what should constitute a naval force under changed conditions. Five years ago there would have been arguments between these gentlemen as to the proper number of battleships as compared with cruisers, cruisers vs. small craft, and so on down the line. Now, however, the argument has got out of the sea and into the air. Sir Percy Scott, for one, declares the battleship is dead and gone, gone indeed previous to the opening of the late war. Why build battleships, says the Admiral, at a cost of say forty million dollars each, when for the same sum many aeroplane-carrying ships, equipped with aeroplanes, each ship carrying explosives in amount equal to that contained on a battleship, could be had. In the opinion of Sir Percy Scott this class of craft would be far the most effective with the added recommendation that plane-carrying ships could be well utilized in peace times as every day, traders, conveying passengers in place of bombs.
Admiral Fisher for his part favours the development of the submarine, which, with the further development of the flying boat will unquestionably be a great factor in future naval engagements if we are unfortunate enough to have any.
All this brings up the point as to what Admiral Jellicoe is likely to recommend for us, though it goes without saying that we do not necessarily have to follow the Admiral's recommendations, no matter what they may happen to be. And if these recommendations follow old traditional lines we may pass them all up. There is no need for Canada to hurry along in such a matter; indeed, there are many questions which are better suited for discussion at the next session of 'Parliament than a definite naval policy for Canada. The best thing Union Government can do is to leave it alone.
Now, let us see what the Prime Minister says in regard to- a naval policy at this time. In the month of December last a deputation composed of representatives of -the Navy League of Canada c-ame to Ottawa to -interview the Government. I will not read the whole of the report which I have before roe, -but here are some of the things that the Prime Minister said:
In reply Sir Robert Borden acknowledged the public spirit and loftiness and purpose that animated the members of. the Navy League of Canada, and complimented them on the patriotic work they are accomplishing.
I may say here that the Navy League asked the Prime 'Minister what- he thought we should do in Canada with regard to naval matters. This report continues:
He called the delegates' attention to the fact that his stand on the naval question had been made public some years ago, and that Interim developments had not caused him to revise the opinions he had expressed at the time.
Now, Sir, we all know what the Prime Minister's stand on the naval question was. He thought that the people of Canada should icontritoute $35,000,000 towards a centralized British navy; he did not want a navy for this country. In December last the Prime Minister reiterated that statement. He practically .said that we did not want a Canadian navy; that he stood by -his old policy, which was to give money to the British Government in connection with their navy. Kef-erring further to the Prime Minister's remarks on this occasion the report says:
The question to solve is one of finance. Sir Robert spoke of Canada's tremendous commitments, the heavy drafts on the country's revenue to meet the interests of war costs, the payment of pensions and other obligations arising out of the war.
Evidently the Government then had no intention to make any expenditures on account of naval services this year.
Let us go a little further. As the Minister of Naval Affairs has pointed out, we had the pleasure and the honour of a visit from Admiral Viscount Jellicoe of Scapa. With

others I had the pleasure of listening to a speech delivered by him at Halifax at a dinner *which was tendered him there. I was more than pleased when during the course of his speech he practically said, though he did not specifically mention the Laurier navy policy, that the only navy which would suit Canada was a navy along the line of that proposed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1910.
Lord Jellicoe, after investigating conditions in this country, made a report. It was .current talk that the Minister of Naval Affairs intended to accept the report of Lord Jellicoe .and to introduce into .the House new legislation or sufficient) Estimates to provide a navy along the lines suggested in that report. The moment this announcement went out in the press protests came in from all parts of Canada, to Conservative and to Liberal members alike, denouncing the policy laid down by Lord Jellicoe. It is well known what happened when we came here in March. Of course, what goes on in caucus is secret, and as I was not at the Conservative caucus to. which I am about to refer I cannot speak with authority as to what happened, though in a moment I will read what a certain gentleman said who was at the caucus. But it was common talk around the corridors, about the city and in the newspaper press that the Minister of Naval Affairs wanted the Conservative caucus to accept the report of Lord Jellicoe and to provide for a navy along the lines suggested, but that the minister was turned down good and hard. Now, let us see what the Halifax Herald says about that, a paper published by a member of the other House, Senator Dennis.
What'are his polities?

Oh, he is a good Tory. Here is what he says:
The demobilization of the Canadian Naval Service follows a decision of the Unionists caucus held recently, at which, it is stated, the plans of Admiral Jellicoe looking to the establishment of a Canadian Navy were turned down in a decisive manner by those present.
The attitude of the caucus and the decision of the Government to demobilize the Naval Service means that Canada will lose a fleet of ships valued at pre-war figures at ? 16,500,000.
I assume (that he refers here to the ships which the British Government offered to this country. He says also-because there is no doubt that the despatch from Ottawa which follows, published in the Halifax Herald, was written by the Senator from Halifax to whom I have referred:

Ottawa, March 23.-House proceedings are completely dwarfed by interest in the Government's decision to scrap the Canadian navy.
While no. official explanation of the action taken has been offered, 'it is known that the order does not represent merely a departmental decision, but is the considered policy of the entire Cabinet.
In the absence of an official announcement the view in Parliamentary and near-Cabinet circles is that the order is based on three considerations :
1.	That the existing naval organization is useless for purposes of defence, and that consequently all money for its upkeep, (the amount is about $6-00,000 annually) is absolute waste:
2.	That all the time when the country is facing a financial stringency challenging the most rigid economy, expenditure of money for all futile purposes is indefensible; and
3.	That the action taken, merely ridding the country of a lot of junk, does not prejudice, hinder or delay any further naval policy that may be decided upon in the light of subsequent events.
These considerations, beyond question, weigh very heavily with the overwhelming majority in Parliament. The Maritime members (including British Columbia as well as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia), of course, are not inclined to be jubilant over any proposal with slightest suspicion of being "anti-navy", .as they are confirmed believers in strong Canadian naval defence, but they realize that it is useless to breast the strong tide for economy and retrenchment which is sweeping through Parliament at the present time.
Also, there is this consideration, that rightly or wrongly, the suspicion prevails that the personnel of the existing naval organization, with some few notable exceptions, did not represent the high level of capacity and that any policy that will rid the country of such service is not to be lightly condemned.
That is what the Halifax Herald says as regards what the Government purpose doing..
In order to show the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) is not alone in his attitude on this matter, I will read from another newspaper known as the Halifax Chronicle. In April last the Halifax Chronicle in a leading editorial, discussed an editorial which appeared in the Manchester Guardian, of Manchester, England. I will no' Tead the whole of the article, which says in part:
However desirable the possession of a considerable naval organization' may be for the Dominion ready to co-operate in case of need with the British navy, it must be faced with the urgent question-"Can we afford it?" Everybody admits that these are times for shortening, not spreading, national as well as individual sail. "Industry and Thrift" are the watchwords of the hour. Canada has incurred an enormous, not to say crushing, public debt through the war. It promises to be a continuing problem of the utmost difficulty, as far ahead as can now be seen, to secure sufficient revenue to pay interest on our indebtedness and pay for the bare necessities of Government. Could we, with

any justice to ourselves or those who are to come after us, consent to the assumption of large additional burdens which are not absolutely urgently imperative?
I think I have said enough to prove to the hon. member for Parkdale and other hon. members, that the hon. member for Beauce is not alone in his attitude and that throughout the length and breadth of Canada the same sentiment prevails. Even the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Burnham) is not in favour of naval expenditure. All he seems to be afraid of is that we have to vote this $2,500,000 because we have this, what he calls the Laurier navy on our hands. My 'hon. friend evidently was not in the House about an hour ago when the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Ballantyne) distinctly told us that he had scrapped the Laurier navy; that he was putting it up for sale toy tender and contract, and that he intended to sell it. Therefore, there is absolutely no reason why my hon. friend, if he is opposed to naval expenditures, cannot vote against the expenditure of every dollar of this $2,500,000. There is no question that the country cannot afford to expend this amount, and it is not necessary to expend it. What do we find? I am sorry I can not read the minister's exact words, and the reason I wanted the committee to rise and report progress was in order that I might not misquote the minister in any particular. I have to go on from memory. What did the minister say about the ships which he is going to accept from the British Government? What part will they play in the defence of this country in case of war with the United States or any other country? In his statement made some two months ago, the minister said:
The Government has decided to carry on tha Canadian Naval Service along pre-war lines and has accepted the offer of Great Britain of one light cruiser and two torpedo boat destroyers to take the place of the present obsolete and useless training ships, the Niobe and Rainbow.
This afternoon he went further; he told us that this gift which he was going to accept from the British Government consisted of one cruiser, if I remember rightly, of 4,600 tons. The Minister of Naval Affairs might consider a cruiser of 4,600 tons an up-to-date cruiser, but I do. not think any one who has a knowledge of naval affairs will consider a cruiser of 4,600 tons is much of a gift after all. In our country we would call her only a boat, but I suppose the minister knows so much about naval matters that he would call her an up-to-date cruiser. He also told us that the British Government had been pleased to give them two
torpedo boat destroyers. if I remember rightly, of about 1,000 tons, and in addition to these two little cruisers we were to get two submarines from the British Government. How thankful we should be that the British Government is to give us these vessels! Before I forget, I might state that the minister said that he intends to use these destroyers and submarines in fishery protection work. The minister is surely mistaken in making such a statement, and I am surprised that he should have made it. How is he going to use submarines or destroyers in fishery protection work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will the hon. member explain how we cannot use them?

I might state that I have
quite as many rights in this House as the Minister of Naval Affairs has. I understood that we were not to interrupt him when he was making his speech this afternoon, and I would ask him to be good enough not to interrupt me. I will tell the minister how he cannot use submarines in fishery protection work. Perhaps he does not know that submarines are undersea boats; they are supposed to go under water. If the minister intends the submarines to locate schools of mackerel or codfish, they cannot do it unless glass frames are placed in front of the submarines instead of the usual plates, so that the sailors can see the fish as they pass along under the water.
What advantage are these little boats going to be to the people of Canada for naval defence? The minister told us that the Niobe was about 8,000 tons and that would be about twice the size of this little cruiser which he is going to accept from the British Government. As the minister was very positive in stating that the Niobe is obsolete, I want to make a comparison between the Niobe, the Rainbow and other ships, such as the Hochelaga, Canada and others, which the Government has at present, and, if you like, Sir Richard McBride's submarines on the Pacific coast, with the boats the Government is going to get from the British Government. I believe the submarines Sir Richard McBride bought are just as good as the ones we are getting now. The Niobe and the Rainbow are just as good boats for training purposes as the cruisers and the two destroyers of which the British Government is going to make us a present. If I remember correctly, at the time the Niobe was purchased, it was understood that [DOT] she was to be used as a nucleus for a Canadian navy and for training purposes, and when the Liberal Government went out of power in 1911, the

Niobe was being used for that purpose. She was well looked after, well equipped as regards both men and machinery, and she was ready at any time to proceed to sea. Shortly after the Conservative Government came into power, the then Minister of Marine and Fisheries adopted the deliberate policy of allowing the Niobe to go into disuse and disrepair, with the result that when war broke out only a few caretakers were on board the Niobe; her engines and boilers had rusted, and it was six weeks after war was declared before she could go to sea. I say it is a disgrace to the Government and to the Minister of the Naval Service of that day that such a condition of affairs should have existed. If the Niobe had been ready to proceed to sea the day war was declared she would have captured sufficient prizes to pay the cost of war to Canada for the first year. The same thing was true of the Rainbow on the Pacific coast. Instead of being ready to proceed to sea as soon as war was declared, she took weeks to get ready. In spite of the fact that the 'Conservative Government and the previous Minister of the Naval Service allowed the Niobe's and Rainbow's engines and boilers to rust, there is no doubt that the Niobe did good work during the war, as long as they kept her boilers in condition, patrolling the New York and the Newfoundland coasts. -At the time she was put out of commission there was nothing wrong with her. All she needed was to have her boilers re-tubed and a few slight repairs. As far as her hull and machinery are concerned, she would do just as good service as a training ship as the boats the minister purposes to take from the Old Country What service can these new boats we are acquiring give us? The minister told us he intended to use them both on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. While, of course, it is quite true that now-a-days in view of the construction of the Panama canal it will not take so long for a cruiser to get from Halifax to Vancouver as it did in the old days when she would have had to go around the Horn, it seems to me a rather strange thing for the minister to say that he is going to protect our 7,000 miles of coast line by taking this cruiser and these two torpedo boat destroyers from one coast to the other as the occasion requires. There is no doubt at alL that these boats are absolutely useless for defence. No man [DOT] thinks they can be used for protection so far as war is concerned. If war were to break out any time within the next ten years they would be absolutely useless. There is another point. If the Niobe is obsolete, as 
the minister says, how many years will it be 'before this cruiser and these torpedo boat destroyers are obsolete? Everybody knows that in the Navy a new cruiser is considered obsolete within five years and the boats the minister is accepting from the British Government if- they are not obsolete to-day-I think he said they were built in 1916-will be obsolete any time from 1921 on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before we
take recess may I suggest to the minister that as the main naval item is the Supplementary Estimate of $2,200,000, and this item is only $300,000, he allow this item to stand until the 'Supplementary Estimate is before us. That will give us an opportunity to discuss this whole question. There is very little sense in passing now an item of $300,000, if later on vre shall be asked to consider an item of $2,200,000. I think the minister should let this item stand in the meantime.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the hon. member for Lunenburg has not yet completed his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are also a few other speakers on this side of the House.

'I am quite ready to defer
the debate until the Supplementary Estimate is before us. I think the members should also have the opportunity of reading the minister's statement before they can be expected to discuss this matter intelligently. I think the proper thing would be for the committee to rise and report progress.
At Six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at Eight o'clock, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In view of the request of the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Lunenburg that we allow this item to stand until hon. members have had an opportunity to read what I said this afternoon, I am quite agreeable to do that and to take up the Fisheries Estimates.

If the minister has been good enough to agree to my suggestion I am quite satisfied that the debate should be deferred for the present although I am ready to go on.
Item stands.
Fisheries-salaries and disbursements of fishery officers and guardians, fisheries patrol service, and oyster culture, $710,'00'0.
What is the increase for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The increase of $110,000 is made up as follows: Extension of the service, $9,120 and steam patrol boats that we have to purchase $70,000, making $79,120. For reclassification we have put in $25,860; reorganization, $2,120; and unforeseen expenses, $2,900; making $110,000.
What is the necessity for more boats if the minister is going to use the new navy for fisheries patrol service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not wish to return to naval affairs but I was talking about fisheries protection this afternoon. The policy of the department is for the present that in British Columbia, cannery, purse seine, gill net and fishing licenses of all kinds are to be thrown open. That being so, it is necessary for the Government to adopt more rigid regulations and to have [DOT]closer supervision by the inspectors out there. Therefore, it is necessary to ask for $70,000 to provide extra boats to enable our officials to go over that vast territory and see that overfishing does not occur.
How many patrol boats have you on the Pacific coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: On the Pacific, 20; on the Atlantic, 16; and on lake Winnipeg, 1.
How many new boats are being bought?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Three new boats that are for use in connection with the British Columbia fisheries.

I cannot understand why you should be building or purchasing several new boats for this particular purpose when you have twenty patrol boats on the Pacific. Twenty boats would cover a great amount of territory, and I do not see why you should require any more.
If the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is only speaking to the minister across the House we might as well go out because we cannot hear a word.
I was not the architect of this Chamber. If I had been I wquld have arranged for a shorter Chamber so that the hon. member for Halifax (Mir. Martin) could hear my voice as well as I can hear his.
You have lots of lung power; speak up.

I was saying to the minister, and I think the hon. member for Halifax
will agree with me, that we should not spend one dollar more than is necessary in order to patrol the waters of the Pacific or Atlantic. The minister tells us that he has already twenty patrol boats on the Pacific coast.
They served you splendidly during the war.

I am sorry I cannot agree with the hon. member for Halifax. They were of no service at all. They were a lot of bumboats; they did no good. But we are not talking about naval affairs; we are talking about patrol boats for fishery purposes. I think we should try and spend as little money as possible and not spend more on patrol boats when there are twenty already on the Pacific coast. There are not as many as that on the Atlantic coast.
Mr. 'STEVENS: There is a very extended coast line on the Pacific because of the large islands. We have the Queen Charlotte group of islands and the large Vancouver island. That necessitates a great deal more patrolling of the coast line than the straight line mileage of the coast would indicate. It may be 1,500 miles in a straight line, but as a matter of fa'ct we have 25,000 miles of coast line including the islands and long inlets, some of which extend 50 or 100 miles into the land. There is a great necessity for increased fishery patrol service on the Pacific. I heartily commend the minister for providing for this additional protection or patrol. The increase of license fees during the past two years on the Pacific coast covers any additional expense involved in the change. We have a situation there which requires very close watching. The American fishing boats come up from Seattle and fish on the banks off and outside of territorial waters. According to law they are not allowed to use our harbours except for the purpose of shelter in storm and certain other restricted uses. It is necessary that this large -area shall be carefully watched so as not to discriminate against us or to endanger our native industry. There is no wastage in connection with the patrol on the Pacific coast at the present time, and I am sure this is a very wise measure on the part of the minister.
What are the receipts from the fishery licenses on the Pacific coast?
Estimated?
No, what are they now?
They were increased this year.

As far as the Atlantic coast is concerned, there is less necessity for using the patrol than there was formerly. We have no trouble from the American fishermen now. The reason for the patrol on the Atlantic coast was largely on account of the American fishermen, and these are now almost on equal terms with our own because they are freely licensed by the Government, and there is very little need of increasing the expenditure on the Atlantic coast. There is always need of a patrol for enforcing the law against men who break it in connection with the fishing industry. I see that there is an increase of $110,000. I would like to know how that increase has arisen. In regard to the overseers and guardians who are covered by this item, changes have been made in Nova Scotia about which I would like to ask some information from the minister. In my own constituency there were two fishery overseers prior to the change, and I do not think their combined salaries would amount to more than about five or six hundred dollars. I am told that they were dismissed, although they were good officers, and new and inexperienced men were put in their places. The new men may be all right-both of them are returned soldiers and very deserving-but the men that were formerly doing the work, and doing it very well, at small salaries were summarily dismissed and inexperienced men put in their places at, I believe, more than double the salary, that was being earned before. I have seen in newspapers the statement that the staff had been reduced in Nova Scotia, and that there are fewer fishery officers than before. That is not the case in my county. There were only two prior to the change, and there are still two; the only difference is that the expenditure has more than doubled, without, I think, increasing the efficiency of the service at all. Now that is not very satisfactory. I do not know whether that condition is widespread or not, but I would like to know from the minister why he dismissed the men that were doing their work well in the constituency that I have the honour to represent. In fact he dismissed three, one on the coast of Antigonish and two on the coast of Guysborough county, and replaced them by other men who had no experience in the protection of the fisheries and who, as far as I can learn, are not any more efficient than the men he dismissed; in fact they are not even as good officers,

but the expenditure has been very largely increased. Now this is not the time to increase the expenditure, and I would like to hear from the minister why he took that step in my constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
First, I will answer the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), who inquired what was the revenue from fishery licenses in British Columbia. In
1918-	19 the revenue was $59,349.94, but in
1919-	20 the fees for canneries and fishery licenses had been increased and the revenue amounted to $270,698.41.
In reply to my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), I think he is aware that when I became Minister of Fisheries the country was overburdened with fishery guardians, who numbered 843 for the whole of Canada The remuneration these men re-, eeived was anywhere from $28 up to $100 per annum. They did very little * guarding of fish, as far as I can understand, and the appointment of these men was considered a political appointment. I let those 843 guardians go on the 1st of April, 1918, and announced that the policy of the Fisheries Department from that date forward would be to only engage such guardians and overseers as the service actually demanded; we would give them larger remuneration than they had been receiving in the past, but we would only employ them during the season of the year when their services would be actually required. As regards the guardians, we pay them whatever the ruling rate of wages is, but only keep them for the number of days they are actually needed. In Nova Scotia, I find, in the year 1917-18, there were 453 guardians. In 1918-19 the number was reduced to 138, and in 1919-20 there were 165; and we estimate that we shall need 100 for the coming year. I do not kno w whether in my memoranda I have the number of guardians in the hon. member's constituency or not.

I would like to get an estimate of the cost as well as the number of men employed. I might say to the minister that I do not think there is anything new in only paying these guardians for the time they work. That has been the policy ever since I can remember -guardians were paid for the actual number of hours they worked during the season. So the minister has not developed anything new in that regard. However, the question I would like to get answered is whether there is an increase or decrease in the expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That was not the system that I found in operation when I

became minister. I think a guardian got $25 a year and did nothing. Sometimes he received $50 and sometimes $100; and as a general rule these men rendered absolutely no service to the country. I therefore deemed it wise to change that policy, and instead of these being political appointments-that is as regards guardians and overseers-to have them appointed on a business basis. The guardians and overseers now employed are required to give their whole time to their duties, and are paid a great deal more than they formerly were, according to the number of days upon which they render service.
How much are they paid?

I hope the minister will be able to give more definite information on this question. I understand that he has reduced the number of overseers to 100, but he has so enormously increased the salaries paid to them that he will spend a great deal more money than was expended before. I would like to know if this is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have a much smaller number of guardians and overseers than we formerly had. The amount paid for their salaries is not only less than it formerly was but there is a greater degree of efficiency.
What is the salary paid, surely the minister can tell us that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The guardians and overseers are paid according to whatever the current wages are-either $2.50 or $3 a day-and depending upon whether they reside in any part of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or British Columbia.

I hope the minister will be able to give me a little more definite information, because I would like to get the salaries that the former overseers in my constituency received, and the salaries he is paying to the new overseers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Under the old rate the overseer in Nova Scotia received $250 plus ten cents a mile. They now receive $1,020 a year. The overseers are permanently engaged, and guardians are not.

It would appear that the present overseers are paid about five times as much as the former overseers. If this is true my hon. friend is not going to save money even by reducing the number from 150 to 100.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
With the remuneration the overseers get, plus the ten cents a
mile, their salaries run about $300 a year.
I admit that we are now paying more than we did in former times, but the present overseers are very much more efficient than the former overseers were.

Does
the department pay the travelling expenses of those overseers in addition to their salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. They are
allowed only $200 a year for the keep of their horses.
In addition?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Is any allowance
made for gasolene for their motor boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We allow th'em an additional $75 a year.

There is no question that
the minister is correct in stating that when he took charge his department was overmanned in the Outside Service. But that was due to the fact that after the Conservative Government came into power in 1911 they fell over themselves in their eagerness to appoint all kinds of officials, whether those officials were required or not, and some 25,000 were appointed between 1911 and 1917. I presume that when the minister took over the Department of Marine and Fisheries in 1917 he found a' certain proportion of those 25,000 officials in that department, and I think he was quite justified in removing a great many of those superfluous officials, some of whom were being paid, as he said a moment ago, $25 just to	keep them
"good fellows" between elections. But I do not think the expenditure of his department is very much less now than it was when he took charge.
However, I would like to get back to the patrol boats. I agree with the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), that it is necessary to have certain patrol boats on both the Atlantic coast and the Pacific coast, but I am not sure whether it is necessary to have more than twenty boats on the Pacific coast. If forty or a hundred are necessary, I am quite satisfied that they should be supplied, but from information I have received it would appear that twenty boats are ample to look after fishery protection in those waters. There is not a great deal of work for the patrol boats to look after. They have a certain territory allotted to them, and it

is no trouble for a boat to cover from 100 to 150 miles per day, and-
Carried.

It is no use to shout "carried," because gentlemen on this side of the House are prepared to sit here all night if they have any interruptions from members on the other side. In fact, I came back *with my friends determined that the vote for the Naval Service should not go through if it took us all night. And we feel the same in regard to the vote for the Fisheries Service. Therefore I would advise hon. gentlemen who have no interest in these Estimates to keep quiet and let us proceed with the business of the House.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would be quite satisfied to vote an increase for the Fisheries Patrol Service if I thought it was necessary. I cannot see that it is. Iff there is necessity for more boats on the Pacific coast, why sell the Canada and the Grilse? Why not put them on the Pacific coast? The minister laughs, but let me tell him that I know the Canada from keel to truck, and she is the best boat in his department. She did excellent service, as the hon. member from Halifax can tell us, before the war as a fisheries protection boat, and she is still able to continue that service. She can be overhauled for a few thousand dollars, as against an expenditure of $50,000 or $100,000 for a new boat. If members from the Pacific coast think they should have one or two more patrol boats to protect their fisheries, let us use those we have rather than spend money for new boats. As I say, the Canada is an excellent boat, and the Grilse, although perhaps a little extravagant in regard to fuel, is also a good boat, and they might well be transferred to the Pacific coast. As the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has said, we do not want sixteen boats on the Atlantic coast at the present time to protect our fisheries. A few years ago. when the Americans were restricted in their use of our harbours and did not enjoy the privileges which have since been granted to them, it was necessary to maintain a strong fleet of fishery protection boats on the Atlantic coast. I strongly urge the minister before he agrees to the expenditure for new patrol boats for the Pacific coast to get advice from other people who know the local conditions there, and I think he will find that if further boats are required his best course will be to transfer some of our Atlantic boats and thereby save the country several thousand dollars.
[Mr. Duff.l

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is confusing the fisheries protection service with the patrol service. The fisheries protection service, as the hon. member is aware, is to protect our fisheries outside the three-mile limit. This vote has nothing to do with the service in that regard. I am asking for this amount for small patrol boats for use on the numerous streams to be found in the province of British Columbia with its long coast line of 7,000 miles. In addition to the twenty small boats that we have now, this vote is to enable me to hire about forty more, and also to build two small boats for use out there. With our license system-and I think it is a correct one, open to all British subjects of the white race-for the preservation of the rich fisheries of British Columbia, it is absolutely necessary that the patrol system be very much more rigidly carried out in the future than it has been in the past. The Canada or the Grilse would be absolutely useless for service on these small streams. For service outside the three mile limit I agree with my hon. friend that those two boats would be quite suitable, but these are small Patrol boats that we need to enforce our fisheries regulations.

I quite appreciate what the minister says, but boats like the Canada and the Grilse can go up any ordinary stream-they do so on the Atlantic coast to-day-and in addition to protecting our fisheries beyond the three-mile limit they look after our inshore fisheries. It is quite true that 100 miles up-river it might be necessary to have other means of protecting the fisheries, but in such cases it seems to me that boats would not be required. We have certain rivers in Nova Scotia where the fishery guardians do not use boats; they patrol the banks of the rivers. It seems to me that unless this is absolutely necessary, and unless the minister has been well advised, money should not be expended in the purchase of new boats. As I said a moment ago, I do not want to say that this money should not be voted if it is absolutely necessary, but my information is that at the present time there are sufficient boats on the Pacific coast. If a few more are needed, let us take them from the Atlantic coast. I have mentioned only the Canada and the Grilse, but the minister knows we have a number of motor boats on the Atlantic coast, and they could be used out on the Pacific coast instead of

spending a large amount of money for new boats.

I rise at this time to take advantage of our system of debate to say a few things about the salmon fisheries of British Columbia. I regret that I had not . an opportunity of being present when my hon. friend from "Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) was speaking, because I always listen to him with the keenest interest. He knows a great deal about fisheries, and he speaks always with the utmost authority. I am told that my hon. friend is qualifying, or attempting to qualify for that most unlikely event, the attainment to office of the present Opposition and his own holding of the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries.
Thank you.

Things often happen that nobody expects to happen, and if my hon. friend should attain to that position every hon. member will have the greatest satisfaction in knowing that at the head of that department is a man who knows what he is talking about, however great mistakes he may make in criticising .the policy of this Government.
Now, Sir, I wish to say a few words upon a matter which interests very much the part of the country that I come from, and a matter which has been the subject of acute controversy. I refer to the salmon fisheries of British Columbia. I know that some of my colleagues from that province do not concur in the view that I take, but I mean to state my case and to set forth what I think to be the right policy in regard to this important matter. Those who do not know the salmon fisheries of British Columbia, those who do not know anything about the habits of salmon, may be interested to know that salmon are a peculiar fish. They spawn in the fresh water, and after hatching they go out to sea. Every four years the sockeye salmon, the greatest family of salmon that keeps up our salmon industry, return and sport around in the outside waters of the great rivers of British Columbia and then commence to make their way back to the spawning grounds. They struggle from boulder to boulder and from crag to crag until they reach the very stream in which they were born, when they finally sink back in the last hours of propagation. The salmon fisheries of British Columbia were once of very great importance. They are still so, indeed, but the Fraser river fisheries have been seriously depleted. The
great run of fish that annually kept up the Fraser river fisheries came down from the northwestern Pacific until they struck the western coast of Vancouver Island. They followed to the inlet along that coast, some of them going in, but most of them going on in great volume until they struck the strait of Juan de Fuca, they proceeded along the American shore, and then crossed to Puget Sound and the eastern shore of that placid waiter. A few of them went into the Skagit and Snohomish and other streams in that district, but the great bulk of the fish were making for that great mother of fisheries, the Fraser. Well, Sir, a peculiar thing happened. Our American friends, whom I sincerely admire, set about to trap these fish on their way to our great fishery grounds. I do not know whether hon. members are familiar with the construction of fish traps,-huge circles of netted wires with great leads going out some hundreds of yards to lead the fish into the traps. Well, our American friends constructed such traps as these and year by year they caught these fish in immense numbers. They persisted in this foolish extravagance until they had practically destroyed our salmon fisheries. When they had a surfeit of catch they sometimes lifted their pots, as they call them

their nets-and allowed the fish to go on, but by that time the fish were too much bruised and exhausted to contend with the strong currents of the Fraser. I tell you that with a great deal of detail, Mr. Chairman, because that was the beginning of the great depletion of the salmon fisheries of the Fraser. When you hear the cannery men of British Columbia tell you about our fisheries being depleted, you will remember that what destroyed the great fisheries of the Fraser was the salmon traps placed in Puget Sound by the American canners.
This diabolical method of fishing finally depleted, as I say, our great salmon fishery. Late in the summer of 1913 contractors working for Mackenzie and Mann work-, ing on the Canadian Northern line along the southern bank of the Fraser put in a great blast and blasted a huge mass of rock into the Fraser River canyon. The fishery officials of the Canadian Government, as well as those of British Columbia, made every effort to erect fish ladders and thus permit the fish to pass, but their efforts were not attended with much success and that is what "put the kibosh" on the great fishery of the Fraser. That marks the final phase of the great run on the Fraser,-a vast run indeed, the fish coming

in wonderful numbers every fourth year. These circumstances provided an excuse on the part of the canners of British Columbia to advocate that a close season be put on in the northern country.
I notice that my hon. friend (Mr. Duff), in the able speech which he made in the House some time ago, quoted Scripture very freely, and I fear that he must have aroused the enmity of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) who is always so apt in his Scriptural illustrations. Well, the quoting of Scripture very often indicates repentence and sometimes precedes conversion, so I have no quarrel with those who do it. But I noticed that in all the quotations which my hon. friend made, from Genesis to Revelation, he did not produce any authority to show' that the fisheries of the world were set aside for one particular people. But that is what took place in Northern British Columbia. About 1909 or 1910 the Government of the day made a regulation that no additional companies should enter into the cannery business in Northern British Columbia, and it came to pass that this regulation was concurred in by the British Columbia Government. I cannot pause to tell you of the enormities which resulted from this regulation or of the great amount of wrongdoing that ensued.
I may say right here that I dislike raising a controversy of this kind. I myself -was for a long time in the cannery business in British Columbia; many of the cannery men of that province are close personal friends Of mine. So far as that goes, the cannery men are as good manufacturers as any other class in the community. At the same time, wre are face to face with a certain condition in our part of the country. We have essayed to break the monopoly which exists. I am in a hard fight to-night, and I mean to lay about me with [DOT]hard blows no matter who may be hit.
These regulations have been in force for about ten years in Northern British Columbia. The great bulk oif fish has been caught by gill nets and the rest has been caught by purse and drag seine nets, with a few traps. The whole coast, outside of gill-net fishing, w'as parcelled out amongst the canning interests, and this resulted in an exclusive monopoly. You will be surprised, Sir, when I tell you that this monopoly had grown to such an extent that we were not allow'ed to know even about our ov'n fisheries. A Mr. Nickerson of the town of Prince Rupert, a man who had fought a long and noble fight for the principle of open fisheries, last summer asked

a quite ordinary question about what cannery or company had a certain license, and he was told that he could not be answered until the gentleman who regulated the fisheries in that part of the country would write to the chief commissioner in Vancouver, and then it might be permitted to mention how these fisheries of ours were parcelled out. Moreover, when I asked the chief commissioner of fisheries in Vancouver if I might have a map showing the purse seine and drag seine licenses, the canneries, the gill net areas, and how the fisheries were parcelled out, in my district, what do you think he said? He said: " I will give you that, but keep it under your hat." I have a pretty big hat, but I have not a big enough hat to keep this under. Well, I asked him: "Why * must I keep it under my hat?" His reply was: "If you don't, you will raise a lot of trouble." I said: "Why will I raise a lot of trouble? Do not these fisheries belong to the people of Northern British Columbia? He said: "Yes, but it will make a lot of trouble." I must, however, to be honest, say that he finally gave me a huge map, which I put up in my office in Prince Rupert, and from the highways and byways I invited those interested in fisheries to come in and look at the map and see how these fisheries had been parcelled out. That shows to what arrogance this privileged interest had grown and how it had got into such a state of monopoly that nobody seemed .to have any knowledge about what was taking place except the privileged class. I have not consulted with the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), but perhaps he will be able to tell the committee that at one time when only purse seine or drag seine licenses were to be let out in that part of the country, they had to be O.K'd by a politician or member of Parliament. I do not know whether that has been the case during his regime, but I think he is aware that that occurred in times preceding his administration. The whole matter had thus grown into a political intrigue and monopoly, and the privileges had been abused. We have had a long array of commissions in regard to the salmon fisheries of British Columbia, and so far as I know, they have never got anywhere; all the awards have generally ended in favour of the cannery concerns. But a rather unique commission was appointed just before the end of the war-I forget what year it was. One of the gentlemen on this commission was a member of the famous food control; another was a fishmonger

from Toronto, and another was some other man who was supposed to know something about the fishery business. That commission brought in a report recommending that no more licenses be granted for the erection of salmon canneries in Northern British Columbia for a period of five years. But a rather unique feature regarding the matter was that one gentleman on this commission, however much he wished to exclude the rest of his countrymen from the benefits of this industry, provided himself with a good fat license in British Columbia, which license he meant to operate under, but which he did not operate under because he found the tide of public opinion was so strong against him that he did not dare to dc so. That is just an instance of fishery commissions and where they lead one to.
This brings me up to last year and the conference of British Columbia members upon this important question last spring. At those conferences a majority of British Columbia members were for open fisheries, and I can leave that question whether they were or not to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), Mr. Desbarats and Mr. Found, superintendent of Fisheries. But it was then too late to change conditions, and certain stipulations were made to provide for returned soldiers, the stipulations being that a certain percentage of gill nets and boats must be provided for returned soldiers. I wish to call the attention of the committee very especially to that point, because it will have an important bearing upon something I wish to speak of a little later on. Hon. members from British Columbia will bear me out that it was determined that the Department of Fisheries be asked to reserve a number of boats in Northern British Columbia for returned soldiers, and the department complied with this request. I may say that the department was at all times most willing to assist us and the returned soldiers and to help along the rational method of fishing. When, however, this occurred, it was too late to change conditions and we had to go on with the policy upon which we had determined. When Col. Cunningham, Chief Inspector of Fisheries for British Columbia, returned to the coast, and, with that easy familiarity he has with them, told British Columbia canners of the new conditions and stipulations regarding returned soldiers, they " went up in the air," according to his statement, and were going to come to Ottawa and do desperate things to the Government; but they apparently became finally persuaded that a good monopoly in the hand was worth a whole lot of 224
uncertain conditions in the bush, and so they agreed to go on under the conditions that were made as regards returned soldiers. Last fall the minister telegraphed to British Columbia that he was about to declare the fisheries of British Columbia open. The Chief Inspector of Fisheries, Col. Cunningham, was called East, and that is where he enters the scene. I may say that I do not like to criticise the conduct of a public servant, but conditions may arise when one feels that one must do so in the public interest. It is an unfortunate circumstance that as long as I can remember-and I can remember over thirty years of the administration of fisheries in British Columbia-the chief inspector and the principal officers in the Department of Fisheries have been very much in favour of the canneries. I am not going to charge dishonesty, but I will say this, that they have had a cannery mind and their whole attitude has always been in favour of the canners.
When the minister telegraphed to British Columbia that he was about to declare the salmon fisheries of British Columbia open there was great consternation, and people wondered what was going to take place. The salmon canners of British Columbia, however, had been privileged for so long to control the policy of the Department of Fisheries that they seemed to be worrying very little. They began to pour in upon the department and the minister-I am saying this upon my own responsibility-voluminous telegrams asking him to wait until the chief inspector got to Ottawa. Now that was a peculiar thing-this monopoly relying upon the chief inspector of the Fisheries as their great bulwark and mainstay. However, the chief inepector finally came here. I also came here at that time. I was interested in Northern British Columbia, and in our part of the country people take an entirely different view from what they take in Southern British Columbia. I made it my business to come here at my own expense to try and influence the department with my views upon this question. It was one with which I was very familiar, and a business in which I had been engaged for a very long time. I rather think the cannery men were asleep at the switch in regard to that. Well, the chief inspector came here and I can faithfully say that he said everything he could say to urge the Government to pursue the policy that had been pursued in the past; but the Minister of Fisheries stood his ground, he was not going to be shaken from his purpose by the onslaught that had been made upon



him by the great rich cannery companies of British Columbia. So he issued a decree that the cannery enterprise was to be thrown open.
I should like, if I may, to detail, at this point the regulations that were to ensue. It is very difficult to illustrate to the House, especially to those hon. gentlemen who are not familiar with the intricacies of the salmon fishing business, the different modes of fishing that obtain, and the different regulations that have to be made. One of the regulations provided that any British subject should be allowed to procure a gill-net license, but no increase was allowed in the number of gill-net licenses to Oriental fishermen. Of course, those gentlemen who come from the East know that this question of Oriental fishing is a very vital one with us. Well, the minister made a regulation that the number of licenses issued to Orientals for gill-net fishing should not be increased, and I wish the House to follow me very closely on that point.

Did I understand my
hon. friend to saw that any increase in the number of Oriental fishermen was forbidden so far as gill-net fishing was concerned?

Yes. The minister made that regulation, which was in close conformity with public opinion in British Columbia. I would ask my hon. friend, whom I respect very much, just to wait for a few moments when I hope to illustrate in a very vivid way the importance of this regulation.
