Next, drag-seines were to be abolished wherever possible. That was a very good regulation, because, ordinarily, fishing by drag-seines is a destructive method. However, in some places it is quite impossible to catch fish without drag-seines, and in those places they have to be used. It creates a very unfortunate condition, because it is hard for the inspectors to decide just where those drag-seines may be used.
What kind of fish do they catch with these drag-seines?

Salmon. I presume my hon. friend from North Cape Breton knows the method of fishing with a drag-seine. They take out a seine several hundred fathoms long and sweep it along the beach. Then the end is brought in to the beach, bringing in the fish. That method of fishing obtains only in certain places.
Next, a drastic change was made in the purse-seine regulations. Here is one of the very important points I want to bring out, and I would direct the very earnest attention of the House
[Mr. Peck. 1
to it. Instead of certain cannery men being granted the exclusive privilege of fishing in large areas the coast was divided into districts, and any white British subject who paid a license fee could obtain a purse-seine license in those areas. That was a very wide departure from the former policy. Not only that, but a future policy was contemplated to remove every vestige of monopoly and restore the fisheries to our own people. I had the pleasure of meeting Col. Cunningham, Chief Inspector of Fisheries, after his return to British Columbia, and he informed me that he thought the new regulations were going to work all right. I told him I was not conceited enough to think that the cannery men had played their trump card, and that proved to be true. I think things would have gone better if the chief inspector had made a more loyal and energetic attempt to support the regulations then in force. That was his proper course. He came here quite properly, ter present his views and argue his point, but when he found that his minister had decided upon different regulations and upon a different policy, then it was his business, if he was in loyal support of his minister and department to go back to British Columbia and try and put his minister's views into operation. That is where the whole thing fell down in my opinion. Instead of that, he seemed to me to do everything to interpret the regulations in the most awkward way and in a way that would disgust every one he could. I hope the minister will see fit at some time to call for the correspondence between the chief inspector and the cannery men. He will find some remarkable corespondence there, if it is all sent to him, which I very much doubt. I am not going into that, but I could entertain the House in a lively manner with some of the correspondence I had the advantage of reviewing.
Up in my part of the country the attitude is entirely different from what it is in Southern British Columbia. I represent what is known as No. 2, of the fishery districts of British Columbia. There are three districts altogether, and all of No. 2 district is in my own riding of Skeena. By a return that was brought down by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries this session I see that the value of the fish caught in British Columbia in 1919-I shall not detain the House by giving the quantities, and I shall give the figures only for salmon, although No. 2 district has the same preponderance in other fisheries that the figures prove it to have in salmon-was as follows: In the Southern district the value of the

salmon amounted to $2,483,897; in Vancouver Island, which is known as No. 3 district, $3,691,123; in my own district, the Northern district, No. 2, the value amounted to $4,744,939. This shows the great preponderance the district I have the honour to represent has In the salmon fisheries of British Columbia. Although we possess these in our own districts they are parcelled out down in Vancouver by the Chief Inspector of Fisheries and we know nothing whatever about what takes place until the gentleman who represents the Fishery Department in our part of the country-and I cannot trust myself to speak any more specifically about him- comes up and informs us as to how these fisheries have been parcelled out. For fear that I may be charged with sectionalism, I shall not pursue the subject any further.
We should have a permanent resident inspector, a man who is all the time on the ground looking after this great fishery-one of the greatest fisheries in the world, really the greatest fishery in the world-in Northern British Columbia. We should have a responsible inspector from whom we could at all times obtain information. I do not mean to criticise the department on that account because we all feel a great deal of gratitude to the minister for the strong stand he has taken in regard to open fishing.
The cannery interests got very busy and manipulated a lot of organizations in Southern British Columbia to petition the minister to cancel any regulations made or to allow those of 1919 to stand for this year, and then have a board appointed to manage the British Columbia fisheries in the future. I regret very much to say that this movement extended to some of the organizations of returned soldiers. In the year 1919 some quite valuable privileges were allotted to different people in British Columbia, some of these people being returned soldiers and therefore these few men became a privileged class and they wanted to keep the thing on. So these associations sent voluminous telegrams-most of them "collect"-to the minister about the fisheries and urging a continuation of the regulations of 1919. All they wanted was one more year, just one more year-anything might happen in one more year; the Government might be defeated-
Hear, hear.

-.and hon. gentlemen opposite might come in, and that is what they really wished to happen, because these opposite canners were the gentlemen who 224*
established this monopoly under the Laurier Government. The cannerymen in British Columbia were very glad to take a chance for another year. However the Minister of Fisheries stood his ground against all these influences, and was determined that these regulations that he had made should stand. That is the end of my narrative in regard to the history of these fishery regulations, how they have come about from time to time and how they have passed from Administration to Administration and Government to Government.

I wish to help my hon. friend to emphasize the case he is making out. Does he mean to tell this committee that the minister had made certain regulations that were satisfactory to him but that the Government official refuses or fails to carry them out?

The minister did make
regulations which were satisfactory to my part of the country and which I think were very strong and statesmanlike regulations. I am criticising the policy of the chief inspector. I have not asked the minister as to his opinion but I am criticising the chief inspector and I attribute to the policy that was pursued by the chief inspector the fact that there is so much discontent now in regard to these regulations.
My understanding is that the officer has not carried out the regulations. Is that correct?

I can only say what I have said already, that his interpretation of the regulations provided the reason for the discontent. One great stock argument is the depletion of the fisheries, and the Fraser river is pointed to. I think I have proved that it was the avarice of the American cannery men on Puget sound that destroyed the Fraser river fisheries and not the gill netter. I have not seen anybody who maintains that the fisheries were destroyed by any other method than trap fishing of the Americans on Puget sound. Yet they will come forward with the most extraordinary arguments, which I shall expose in a few minutes. It has been argued that the Alaskan fisheries are being depleted. That may be true, and it is due to the same unscrupulous use of traps by the Alaskan cannery men. One thing that is most peculiar with our friends to the south of us is their remarkable indifference to their natural resources. They seem to wish to go ahead and manufacture everything they can regardless of the future supply. The same

condition obtains on the Naas river. The mouth of the Naas river is contiguous to the Portland canal and one side of the Portland canal is in American territory. Our American .friends are constructing traps along the northern part of the Portland canal and catching a lot of our Naas fish. No doubt they will injure or destroy that great fishery. If everybody fishes at every place and fishes as hard as he can, it will destroy any fishery, but if you make regulations' [DOT] that there shall be certain close seasons and that nets cannot be cast in certain areas you will allow the fish to pass up to the great spawning grounds.
Now we come to some of the criticisms which have been made with regard to these fishery regulations of the minister. Let us take the arguments which are made by those who are opposing the new regulations. We listen to what is said by Mr. Peter Wallace, the pioneers in the northern portion of British Columbia, a man whom I know very well and of whom I think very highly in his private character. But he has always taken a very peculiar view of the fishery situation. He claims that these new regulations will destroy the fisheries of British Columbia, and is thus quoted in the Vancouver World:
I venture to say that hardly a cannery will operate this side of the line. The owners will strip their plants to get out of them what they can.
That is the dictum of Mr. Peter Wallace, one of the pioneer fishermen of British Columbia. In the first place, I direct the minister's attention to the fact that any argument that is put up by a canner man should be discounted by seventy-five per cent because it is argument in which he is personally interested. But I should discount the .argument of Mr. Peter Wallace by more than that. I have known him for * a long time, and the underlying point of the . argument he has always put up has invariably been this:	God put the fish
into the sea for the sole benefit and emolument of the Wallace people. That has always been the nature of his argument. Now he, and some otheT gentlemen who are associated with him, talk about the fishing out of the fisheries of British Columbia. I want to ask one question-and in this connection I appeal to my colleagues from British Columbia:	Who fished out
-or very nearly did- Smith's inlet? My hon. friend from Comox (Mr. Clements) will know something about that. Who fished out Barclay sound and Naden harbour? Who but this gentleman and

liis associates. Who, twenty years ago, fished out the sturgeon fisheries-in cold blood-of Pitt lake? Who but this gentleman and his associates. He talks about the Americans, but in the nineties he was over helping *o fish out the poor old Columbia river. But the Columbia river fisheries recovered, just as surely as ours will recover with a proper system of conservation. However, that is the class of argument that we encounter with some of the canners of British Columbia.
Now, I shall cause Mr. Wallace to leave the stage and we shall have another entry up it-I will not say the entry of a hero, neither will I say of a villain-I refer to Hon. William Sloan, Minister of Fisheries of British Columbia. He is always there with the corporations, ready to raise a voice in the interests of privilege. When these new regulations were made by the minister -I will let you into a Calrnet secret, I do not. think I am acting wrongly in so doing -the Minister of .Fisheries of British Columbia tried to induce the British Columbia Cabinet to condemn those regulations. But " Honest John " and some of his friends did not see it that way, so he had to decide upon another policy. He brought out a very elaborate treatise which was very well printed. Its cover, if I remember rightly, was ornamented with gold lettering. iThis treatise stated that the fisheries of British Columbia were about to be entirely depleted, and he advocated that the Government of Canada should take them over. What a pity it is that these views about the cannery monopoly did not once cross Mr. Sloan's mind when he was a member of the Dominion Parliament and a supporter of the Laurier 'Government. What a pity it was that it did not cross his mind in view of the fact that he, more than any other living man, was responsible for the introduction of this canning monopoly in Northern British Columbia. I remember very well-I was in the cannery business myself at that time-his telling me about how they were going to prevent any other canneries being started on the Skeena and on the northern rivers. I said to him, " Bill, it's too raw, the people won't stand for it." However, I was wrong and he was right. The people did stand for it all these years, and a lot of them stand for it yet; so I was wrong in that regard.
Now, Sir, I have nothing against that argument, if it can be proven that private enterprise cannot handle these fisheries. I belong to that school of economists who think that these are natural resources of

the country which by their nature may be very well and to advantage administered by the Government; but if any one can prove to me that the fisheries of British Columbia may be better operated by the Government I would be very glad to support that argument and that plan. However, I do not believe, Sir, that that is the case. Take our Atlantic fisheries. I might appeal to my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) and my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) who know those fisheries well, and I think they will admit that they are carried out entirely by private enterprise. Furthermore those fisheries are very successful, they are a great resource of this country, and there is no reason why they should be carried on and operated by the Government.
I would like to read a quotation from a speech that was made by Hon. Mr. Sloan at the Fisheries Convention that was recently held in Vancouver, and I am sorry that 1 have not got time to read it in extenso, he said in part:
I view with alarm existing conditions. There is the gravest danger of one of our leading assets being wholly destroyed. It is time the Dominion Government viewed the situation in this province as it is. Commission after commission appointed by the Dominion, after investigation, have set forth the distressing facts.
The reports and recommendations of those commissions have been and are being ignored in Ottawa.
Of course Mr. Sloan does not say how long this ignoring has taken place, but it is some time. He goes on:
It is high time that the conditions be realized. The fish of the province belong primarily to its people and the people of Canada.
That is the particular phrase I wish to call attention to. Mr. Sion did not' have those views when he induced the Laurier Government to introduce the cannery monopoly. Oh, no, he did not have those views at all. He then thought that those fisheries should be left to the canners of northern British Columbia. He suddenly experienced a change, but we are very happy to see that illustrious statesman arrive at such a state of mind. He continues:
They constitute one of their greatest natural resources. The fisheries, if properly administered, will last for all time. They can be so administered as to outlast our mines and our forests. The depleted runs can be restored. The interior lake waters can be stocked with desirable forms of food fishes without danger '.a existing species.
He was very hopeful so long as we kept the great fishery in the hands of a private monopoly. He goes on:
The salmon fisheries of this province should be taken over bodily by the Dominion Government and operated to their betterment.
As I said before, what a shame it is that Mr. Sloan did not have those views when he got the cannery monopoly established. However, he has changed his mind and when the cannery monopoly came under the firm hand of a strong federal minister he comes out and says: "Let us hand the thing over to the Government". I have a very strong suspicion, Mr. Chairman, that there are some very bad old cannery plants on the Fraser that the owners wish sold at a good price. I think there is a whole lot to be said from that point of view.
I would like to put this question to the committee, whether or not they think that I or the other residents of northern British Columbia are going to advocate a policy which will destroy those great fisheries. I do not think that any hon. gentleman will accuse us of anything like that. We want to open those fisheries to the enterprise of our countrymen.
I wish to quote from a letter written to me by a man whose name is very honourably associated with the salmon fisheries of British Columbia, a man who has passed the best part of his life in the industry, and who wished to get a cannery license. In his letter he quotes what a cannery man,-not a fishery official remember,-said to him:
I will give you $5,000-
This is in regard to a cannery license which a cannery company wished to secure in certain waters of northern British Columbia.
I will give you $5,000 in cash or stock if you get that license. I will have no dealing with anyone else in the matter. If you do not accept this you will not get the license.
This, of course, was some years ago. I could quote a whole lot more, Mr. Chairman, but I think I should not detain the House at this hour. I say that this monopoly not only debauches the people who regulate it, but it debauches the people who enjoy it, for it leads to all sorts of intrigue and machinations, and ultimately it can lead only to corruption.
Let us come to the chief argument that has been advanced by the cannery interests against the purse-seine regulations of the minister. Of cpurse they did not say fhat what they feared was the destruction of the cannery monopoly. No! what they feared was that this purse seining would get in the hands of the Japanese! It is very edifying to find the cannery men so

anxious for the benefit of the white men. I appeal to anyone and to all my hon. friends from British Columbia as to how the Oriental prestige in our salmon fishing grew up, how but under the fostering care of the salmon canners of British Columbia. Can any man deny that? I think not. That is how they grew up, but all of a sudden those gentlemen become exceedingly patriotic and they do not want to see purse seining get into the hands of the Japanese ! They claim that by opening up the purse-seine areas- instead of keping them for their own exclusive monopoly-they, the cannery men, will be able to get all kinds of purse-seine licenses in the name of white British subjects and then employ Japanese to run them. However, Sir, they have been playing upon the fears of several organizations, and they have induced those organizations to take action, at least, we have all received long "collect" telegrams- (all hon. members from British Columbia who remain here for the magnificent sum of $2,500)-costing $4 or $5 each, asking us to preserve the regulations of 1919. I wish to say that the policy of the minister in making those regulations was to destroy this monopoly and to restore our fisheries to our own people.
Now I wish to come to what I think is a very important point. As long as I have been in British Columbia, and that is oveT 30 years, I have heard politicians year in and year out seeking to represent the people in municipal, provincial and federal affairs, and their one line of talk has been to make the province a "white British Columbia." But I notice that the province is getting more yellow all the time. At last comes along a minister who, I venture to say, proposes to pursue a definite policy which will restore these fisheries to our own people. What happens? The interests who enjoy the privileges of this monopoly turn against him. Not that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wishes to discriminate against the Japanes people. I do not think that is in his mind; I am sure he has the same admiration for the Japanese nation as I have myself. I adimire the prompt way in wdiich they entered into the war; I admire their punctilious observance of treaties; and I admire the honourable way in which they discharged their obligations in the war. But at the same time I think it is ridiculous to say that Japan would ever tolerate a state of affairs such as we have in British Columbia where a foreign population controls the fisheries.
Let me make a comparison of how our fishery licenses are allotted between the

Japanese and our native-born Canadians In 1919 out of 4,596 gill net licenses, only 417 were held by native-born Canadians; and out of 2,203 trolling licenses only 412 were held by native-born Canadians. Now these methods of fishing are peculiarly th< poor man's, and I am quoting these figure! to show how the fisheries are controlled by the Japanese.
Shortly after the war regulations were published, Mr. Ukita, the Japanese Consul in Vancouver, got- into 'the press, and he condemned the regulations. But I would like to put it to. Mr. Ukita, with the utmost respect for him or any other representative of the Imperial Japanese Government, if he thinks his government would tolerate a state of affairs such as obtains in our fisheries in British Columbia. I do net think so for a moment. We might cite their mercantile policy. When they started their mercantile marine they had their ships built in Great Britain, but they employed British officers to manage them. As time went along-and no one could criticise their action; it was quite right-they officered those ships with their own nationals, and it is well known now that the ambition of Japan is to control the mercantile marine of the Pacific. No one criticises that ambition. It shows that Japan is a wide-awake nation. It also shows that she would not for a moment tolerate the state of affairs in her fisheries such as we permit in British Columbia by allowing the Japanese to control our salmon fisheries.
There is a great deal of difference of opinion about matters of naval policy. Well, if we ever have a navy or a great mercantile marine, where are we going to draw our sailors from? Are we going to draw them from a foreign population? I put that question to my hon. friend (Mr. Duff). Shall we draw them from Japanese engaged in the fisheries? I do not think so. But, somebody may say, these Japanese who engage in this business-are they not all British subjects? Some of them are and some are not. As I pointed out the other day to a committee of the House, a good many of these naturalization papers are juggled back and forth so that we have no reason to know that it is a bona fide British subject who is securing a particular license.
It is suggested that an embargo be placed upon the export of salmon from British Columbia to the United States, The cannery men want an embargo on certain grades of fish in order to prevent them going to the United States. Personally I see no reason why an embargo should be put on

this product any more than, it should be put on grain or any other similar product. If such an embargo is put on, an exclusive market will be 'Created and the fishermen will not obtain as good a price for their fish as they otherwise would.
The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) made a very able and very instructive speech a short time ago upon the general question of the fisheries, during the course of which he erticised the policy bf articficial propagation of fish. We have no better authority than my hon. friend in the matter of the eastern fisheries, but when he gets into British Columbia he gets beyond Ihjis depth;-the water there is a little deeper than he is accusomed to. I am fair to say that the hon. member would not have made the criticisms that he did had he not been misinformed from certain quarters,-and I really think I know from what quarters he received his information. However, he mentioned the depletion of the sockeye fisheries and the expansion of -production of pinks and chums, the cheaper grades of fish, which have not been propagated artificially. He endeavoured to show a continuous decline in sockeye production and a continuous climb in chum and pink salmon production, with the object of proving that notwithstanding the hatching of sockeye the fishery has been going down and that without artificial hatching the other species have been coming up; in other words, that the hatcheries have been depleting rather than building up the sockeye fisheries. He points out a serious downward trend in the sockeye fishery of the Naas river, but he fails to .state that there never has been a hatchery on the Naas, or that that river system has never been stocked from any hatchery. On the Skeena, where we have two hatcheries, the sockeye fishery is being rapidly brought back to the maximum of productivity. The hon. gentleman's figures stopped at 1917, up to which point there was for many years a general downward trend. But while the pack in 1917 was 65,760 cases of sockeyes, in 1918 it rose to 123,322 cases, and last year to 184,945 cases, (or only about 2,000 -cases less than the biggest pack ever put up in any one year since fishing started there), which was in 1910, when 187,246 cases were packed. Another fact which shows what the hatcheries are doing on this -system is that when the Babine hatchery at -the head of the Skeena river was established, it was placed on a stream which while suitable for a hatchery, was not frequented by salmon to any considerable
extent. After -stocking this stream for a number of years we find that salmon are now coming to it every year in such numbers that the hatchery is usually practically filled from this stream alone. I, cite these facts for the information of my hon. friend. As a matter o-f -fact,, the salmon of British Columbia have been almost entirely controlled by the sockeye pack. The sockeye are the red fish; they are sold in the Old Country market, and that market controls salmon prices just as it controls the prices of many other products. -Such fi-sh as pinks and chums have never been sold in the Old Country market. In fact, they were not manufactured to any great extent in British Columbia until the war conditions came upon us and there was a great demand for cheap food. The -salmon canners of British Columbia then found it profitable to manufacture the cheap grades of salmon, and the trade in these grades has grown to a considerable extent. But artificial propagation had -nothing to do with the growth of production of these grades; I think my hon. friend will find that I am correct if he looks carefully into the matter.
With regard to the policy of the department, I hope that returned soldiers will be given an opportunity of entering into fishery enterprises. I -shall not go into this matter in detail, because it is now before a committee of the House and it is not proper that I should speak upon it now at any great -length. But I hope that -some such policy will be adopted.
T-o sum up: I make bold to -say that the discontent in British Columbia over regulations-outside of the manipulations of -those who were personally interested-was caused by the interpretation that wa-s put upon them by the Chief Inspector of Fisheries. Had he interpreted them according to the spirit of the minister's policy he would have had little trouble. But what has been the result? The cannery men say that if you throw these fisheries open so that everybody has -the right to come in, there will be a lot of canneries and the fisheries will be depleted. Well, since the minister broke this monopoly one canner has started business in my -di-strict. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that before this monopoly was broken three different canners came -to me and asked me to assist them to secure licenses in No. 2 district. So you can see that these men were willing to -start so long as they had a monopoly, but once the monopoly was broken they were not willing to take a chance with the outside world.

The result is that recently fewer canneries have been started than would have been started had these gentlemen achieved their desire. I think, therefore, it is proved that in such competition as obtains in Nova Scotia and the Maritime Provinces, where people enter the business without any favours, competing openly with the world, there is a natural safety valve which regulates the enterprise; and that under such conditions the fisheries will not be destroyed.	.
What we want in this country is a great white fishing population, men of our own brawn and breed, men who will develop this great enterprise so that it will be our mainstay in the hours of national peril. I appeal to this Government and to any Government, and to this Parliament and to any Parliament to stand by the regulations of the minister. I do not claim that those regulations are perfect, but if they are wrong they can be changed. If it can be proved that this industry cannot be operated by private enterprise, I would be prepared to see the Government take it over, [DOT] but it must be proved to me first. Whatever happens, I wish to appeal to the committee not to put us again under the heel of this monopoly. Leave this enterprise open to the enterprise of all our citizens and do not exclude us from this great natural resource which has been bestowed upon us by a Divine hand for our sustenance, prosperity and happiness.

I am sure we have all been greatly interested in listening to the remarks made by my hon. friend (Mr. Peck), whose address will be a valuable contribution to Hansard. With his knowledge of Pacific fisheries, especially the salmon fisheries, we are all pleased to listen to his observations. I am glad to hear that the salmon fishery monopoly in British Columbia has been, done away with, and I might say to my hon. friend that some hon. members on this side of the House who, if they only had the power, would, perhaps, long ago have broken this monopoly, appealed to the minister that it was time this monopoly was broken. If hy hon. friend will refer to Hansard of March, 1919, he will find that when the Fisheries Act, 1914 was being amended in regard to licenses for .salmon canneries in British Columbia, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and your humble servant, the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), strongly advised the then Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. A.

K. Maclean), who was in charge of that Bill that the monopoly at that time existing in British Columbia was not in the best interests of the fisheries. In the Montreal Star I noticed a report of an address made by the Hon. Mr. Sloan, Minister of Fisheries of British Columbia at the annual convention of Fisheries in Vancouver. That gentleman strongly criticised the Minister of Fisheries regarding the Fisheries of British Columbia; he held that the officials on the coast were not men wn* should be in charge of the fisheries. I also note from what my hon. friend (Mr. Peck) says, that he is evidently not quite satisfied with the fishery officials on the British Columbia coast. The hon. gentleman will remember that when I made my few remarks in March, 1920, regarding the fisheries, I strongly represented to the minister and to Parliament that some change should be made in regard to the officials who had charge of the fisheries on both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. I am very glad my hon. friend has backed me up in that view. The time has come when we should have practical men in charge of the fisheries of this country. If we ever expect our fisheries to progress and increase, and people to engage in this great industry, we must have, in charge of the fisheries on either the Pacific or the Atlantic coast, men who have practical knowledge, so that when the public come before them those officials will be able to give them practical advice. We appreciate what my hon. friend has told us regarding the fisheries. He has made a very illuminating address, and I am sure the committee has listened with pleasure to his observations.

If there is one member more than another for whom I have a kind regard, it is the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff), but when he tells this committee that the Canada and the Grilse should be maintained for fishery purposes in streams and rivers, then he and I disagree. I have not taken up much of the time of this House, and I do not intend to do so now, for two reasons: First, on account of my disability, I could not stand up to express myself as I would wish to do; second, I can tell a story perhaps that will illustrate my position. I had an old friend in Nova Scotia whom I had assisted in placing in a council. He had served there for three years without saying a word, and about the expiration of his time I said to him: "Old man, say something so as to let the people know that you are there." He

said: "It is necessary to be here for three years to know what to say without making a fool of yourself."
Why are you speaking now?

Louder. I would ask my hon. friend (Mr. Duff) if we really have a fishing industry in Nova Scotia. I am sure he will answer "yes," and so will I, and we have a good one, one profitable for him as well as for others. But last year, returning from Ottawa, while I was at Montreal waiting for my train, I dropped into a theatre. About that time the Victory Loan was on and pictures were being thrown on the screen showing why we should purchase bonds, the reason, of course, being that we might assist our Allies, and so on. The pictures started from the West, showing the wheat fields with the magnificent crops of wheat and all the rest of it. Then pictures were shown of the shipping of the wheat to the elevators and the work of loading, and it was said that this was what we were spending the money for in order to assist our Allies. We came, however, from the West to Ontario and Quebec, and very nice things were said about those provinces. But we arrived .at New Brunswick, and on the screen this was said: "New Brunswick is noted for its coal and steel industries." I do not know of any such industries in New Brunswick. Then, we came further East, and we were told: "Prince Edward Island is noted for its immense fisheries. What a joke! I do not know where Nova Scotia was all this time, but that w.as no fault of New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island, for the reason that the then Minister of Finance had a stupid bunch at Ottawa. I inquired where this information was obtained, and I was told: "Oh, the Publicity Committee at Ottawa." That accounts for how that happened. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) said many things in his speech, and he really quoted Scripture. I think he must have been tutored by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) because he quoted to the extent that our Lord had sent Simon to cast the net in which he caught multitudes of fishes. But, perhaps, the net was a little larger at this time, and our Lord went somewhat further and said to Simon: "Go forth; fear nothing; you will catch men later on." I think we have caught the hon. member for Lunenburg not treating this Government fairly for what they have done.
He read and gave us fine, grand advice, but I would ask him: WTas the fishing industry in Nova Scotia worth while in 1910? I think echo answers, yes. What did his friends, the then Minister of Finance, now the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) and the leader of the Opposition in this House to-day (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and the hon. member for Antigon-ish (Mr. Sinclair) do for the fishing industry in Nova Scotia in those days? Nothing that we know of. Then why blame? Why not give credit where credit is due? From 1911 up to to-day many and many good things have been done by this Government for the fishing industry of Canada, and particularly of Nova Scotia. I do not wish to waste the time of this House, as it has been wasted by other hon. members, by putting on Hansard all that has been done by this Governmet for the fishing industry of Canada and Nova Scotia particularly.
Where is Nova Scotia?
It is not in Quebec anyway. I shall not place these facts on Hansard-
Is Nova Scotia-

Sit down. I shall publish these facts as to the fishing industry in the press and they will show that the hon. member for Lunenburg has not given to the Government that credit which is due them, and I hope these facts will make him change his mind in the near future.

While we are on the subject of fishing, having heard from the far West and the 'far East, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the question of net or seine fishing in Missisquoi bay. Two years ago I brought before the House and before the minister the .question of the prohibition of net fishing in Missisquoi bay. The inhabitants of the country surrounding this bay have long been accustomed to fish with seines for six weeks in the spring of the year, from the 1st of March to the 15th of April. A great many of these men earn their livelihood from this pursuit. I have estimated that at the present price of fish the catch of these fishermen in the six weeks would amount to $21,000. But this Government, by an Order in Council passed on the 18th of February, 1918, prohibited net fishing in Missisquoi bay. The Order in Council was based on the advice of the Interntional Joint Com-

mission on Fisheries, and I have before me the evidence taken .before that commission which was brought down in a return a few days ago. The Canadian members who sat upon that commission were: Mr. Hazen, now Chief Justice of New Brunswick; and Mr. Found, of the department here. I am surprised to find by the evidence that the only witnesses heard were representatives of the states of Vermont and New York. The Canadian members of the commission did not think it was necessary even to invite any Canadians who were conversant with the situation in Missisquoi bay, to refute the evidence given before that commission by these other witnesses. I am going to read a few extracts from the evidence. The first is headed "The Lake Champlain situation":
Chairman Redfleld:	I understand that our
friends from Vermont, who are interested in the lake Champlain situation, are here, and we shall be pleased to hear from them.
The first witness called was Commissioner Patrick, representing the Vermont Fish and Game League. Mr. Patrick seemed to take the ground that as the United States had become our Allies in the war it was only proper that this country should grant any request made by the United States. This is what he says:
If there was ever a time in the history of this North American continent when Canada could ask a favour of the United States or when the United States could ask a favour of Canada, it would seem to me that that time is the present, when our boys are fighting side by side with your boys and when both countries are linked together in an effort to win a world-wide war for democracy. With the present good feeling that seems to exist between the two countries, for that reason, we feel that we now have a right to ask that the seining or drawing of nets in Missisquoi bay be discontinued, and we hope this request will receive impartial and careful consideration and will be granted.
The next witness was Fish Commissioner Linus Leavens, Chairman of the Vermont State Fish Commission. He says:
Our people are very much interested in the development of the inland waters of lake Champlain as a source of supply for food and game fishing.
The next witness was Mr. Loomis, Chairman of the Lake Shore Transportation Company. He says:
I am engaged in the operation of hotels and steamboats on lake Champlain. Our business is largely that of a tourist character, and among the tourists a large number are hook and line anglers. Their attention is attracted to Vermont because of the hook and line angling in lake Champlain. The continuation of the seining has had a very serious effect on hook and line fishing.

This argument is not a good one, as I think I can prove to the minister.
It is now three seasons since seine fishing has been abolished in Missisquoi bay and to-day there are fewer sporting fish than there were three years ago. The reason is this: Missisquoi bay has a great number of fish know as perch. This is a small active fish that feeds on the spawn and young minnows of other breeds. Out of the total catch of fish in Missisquoi bay 82 tons were perch and about 17 tons wall-eyed pike or dore which is the fish the Vermonters wish to preserve for their tourist traffic. You can readily understand that if these large numbers of perch are left to breed and increase in the lake they will very soon entirely destroy all the game fish. At present that lake is absolutely infested with perch. The angler drops his line in the bay, swarms of perch crown about his bait and he gets a small fish weighing about half a pound.
The next witness before the commission was Mr. Titcomb, Fish Commissioner of the State of New York. He says:
Here on lake Champlain there are millions of dollars Invested in summer homes and hotels, and certainly something should be done in the way of protection. The pike-perch is looked on in this lake as a game fish. It is one of the few places in the country where the pike-perch is regarded as a game fish. It is a great thing for that section to have people able to catch them.
In the course of his evidence further on he says:
Missisquoi bay elects representatives on the issue, also, the same as is done on our side. Your fishermen elect members of Parliament by campaign funds on this issue, and the same thing is done by fishermen in Vermont in connection with the Vermont legislature, and men on our side assist in helping your members of Parliament to get elected, to keep up fishing on that side.
I may say that as far as I am concerned that is entirely untrue. I received no assistance from the American at the time I was elected. Mr. Titcomb says further:
If we can get the rough fish out of the lake-
Rough fish being the perch and others like the bullpouts.
-without interfering with the fish tha{ bring these people into the region and that have brought in property there so that it has increased from a very small, nominal value to an immense amount, increasing the wealth of the surrounding country by bringing in beautiful homes, well and good.
Even this Vermont commissioner realizes the fact that these rough fish should be taken out of the lake. At the end of the evidence:

Commissioner Hazen: Are there any other States that border on the waters of lake Champlain except Vermont and New York?
Mr. Titcomb: No. Sir.
Commissioner Hazen: And has all fishing been abolished there?
Mr. Titcomb: All net fishing.
Commissioner Hazen: Net fishing, as well as seine fishing?
Mr. Titcomb: Yes, sir, every kind.
This is the way commissioner Hazen sums up:
We have listened; gentlemen, especially Mr. Found and myself, the Canadian members of the Commission, with very much interest to what has been said by you gentlemen from New York and Vermont, and I have no hesitation in saying that I think they have made out a very strong case.
Further on he says:
I think, in view of what you have said, that the matter will be taken up by the Canadian department dealing with fisheries, and X feel that they will be impressed, as Mr. Found and myself have been impressed, by the facts presented. I think very little time will elapse before the question will be fairly met, with the idea of preserving the fish in the lake. While we have not heard what may be said by the people on the Canadian side with regard to this matter, it appears to us at the present time that this fishing by nets should be abolished and that only fishing by hook and line should be allowed. In that way the fish will be preserved and those waters will continue to be a source of delight to tourists who enjoy the fishing. I think in the long run such action as is suggested will be very much in the interest of all.
Our commissioner, the present Chief Justice of New Brunswick, commented upon the fact that no Canadians had been called to give evidence but he dismissed that with a wave of his hand. Is that the position wich our representatives on the International Joint Commissions take as regards the rights of Canadians? In the course of some of the correspondence which took place between the department of Marine and Fisheries and the Fish Commissioners of Vermont and New York there are a few extracts I would like to read to the committee. Here is a letter from Mr. Loomis to Mr. Titcomb:
We want to all pull together, and it seems to me as if we can break up this piratical crowd of Canadians in Missisquoi County. They and the fish buyers are probably the only ones who are anxious for this thing to go on. There is work yet to do on this question, and I trust you will continue to give us your valuable assistance.
Here is a copy of a letter received by Mr. Loomis from a friend located in Alburg, Vermont which is situated on the American side of Missiquoi bay:
The pirates are all at work. They are chopping ice preparatory to fishing In a large scale. Shanties are all placed, large gangs of men are
chopping in order to make the first haul March 1st. Ice awful thick. Above in response to telegrams received Saturday and yesterday from Quebec to ''go ahead". Licenses are on the way.
Naturally the Canadian fishermen are jubilant, and often remark "to H... with the d... Yankees and Ottawa Government. Quebec can ruu their own business", etc., etc. Likewise the American fishermen are mad. thoroughly mad, and the question is, "We'll get all we can. Fish buyers from Boston and New York are here on every train.
That letter was sent to Mr. Desbarats Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries and in acknowledging it to Mr. Titcomb Mr. Desbarats uses this curious language:
You are no doubt in a position to closely follow the conditions through your local officers, and if you will inform me of any steps being taken towards irregularities we should endeavour to see that the necessary measures are taken to have the law fully enforced.
In order that the minister may be fully seized of the geography of lake Champlain, I wish to correct a statement made in an official communication from him. I hold in my hand a letter written by the minister on this question in which he states:
But a small portion of the lake is in Canadian territory, and the States of Vermont and Massachusetts in which by far the greater portion of it lies,-
I wish to point ont to the minister that lake Champlain is bounded on one side by the State of Vermont and on the other by the State of New York.
In view of the fact that this Order in Council was passed at the request of the United States authorities, espcially the authorities of the States of Vermont and New York, and was practically granted by our section of the commission owing to the fact that they were our allies-of course it seemed that as such we must grant them every request they made-and in view of the fact that no Canadians (none of the fishermen and none of the people from this side of the line) were consulted or asked to give evidence before the commission, I ask the minister if he does not think it would be fair to re-open the case and heaT what our people have to say. If he will grant that request, I can produce a great deal of very interesting evidence. The fishermen on this side of the line who come to Missisquoi bay for the purpose of catching bass-of which there were formerly a great many in the lake-all assure me that since seining has been prohibited bass and pike-perch have decreased very much, while perch have greatly increased. As I said before, there is a very insignificant number of pike-perch caught with seines in the spring, as seining is stopped on the 15th April at the time the

fish have commenced to spawn. The people of the country surrounding Missisquoi, by the permitting of seining, would 'be supplied with a great quantity of good, fresh fish at a season of the year when it is veTy much in demand, and the anglers would enjoy very much better fishing if this vast quantity of perch could 'be taken out of the lake every year. Two years ago, at the time I brought to the attention of the minister the fact that this seining had been going on for a great many years, I stated that the fishermen were accustomed! to prepare for their fishing a week or two in advance, that many of them at that time had bought new equipment which represented to them a considerable amount of money, and that the Order in Counoil prohibiting seine fishing was passed on the 18th February, and only published on the 26th of that month, four days before seining was to commence. I then asked the minister if he could not see his way clear to recommend the reimbursement to these men of the amount they had spent in purchasing new equipment. I am sorry to say the minister could not see his way clear to granting that request, and these men still have their seines unused. They have not broken the law in any way, they have observed the rules which the Government made by Order in Council, and therefore I appeal to him very strongly to have the case re-opened, or better still to immediately pass an Order in Council restoring the rights which Missisquoi bay enjoyed in former years.

I propose to detain the committee very briefly indeed while I offer a few observations in support of the case made out by the hon. member for Missisquoi for the re-opening of this question of seining for fish in Missisquoi bay I can quite understand that at the first glance, after only a cursory examination of the subject, it would appear that if you stop netting fish in any great body of water there would be more fish which would be caught by hook and line. But it would appear that the experience of the last few years is to the contrary; that in lake Champlain the prohibition of seining for the rough, or less valuable, breeds of fish has resulted in their very great increase, and in the comparative decrease of the game fish-the black bass, the pike, and fish of that character. Now it would appear that no one could object to the object of this legislation. The object was to develop the game fish in lake Champlain I have to remark, however, that the regu

lation in question was arrived at on very slight evidence and without proper opportunity to the Canadian fishermen to present their case. However, it is rather to the future than to the past that I wish to look. I would like to see this matter reopened. I would like to have the question looked at in the light of the experience that the last three years have afforded, because it does seem to me reasonable to argue that if the rough fish are taken out of this lake there will be more food for the game fish, and the spawn of those fish will be protected from the ravages of the coarser varieties. This is a matter which does not merely concern the fishermen at Missisquoi, whom to characterize as "pirates" is very improper; they are very decent people who live there and earn their living in the summer through acting as guides and fishermen, and who fish in the early spring in a commercial way and are able to make a decent livelihood for their families in that manner. But there is a more important feature of the situation, and it is this: There has been a tremendous development on both sides of lake Champlain by summer resorts. But lake Champlain-beautiful lake as it is- is only somewhat as beautiful as the country that lies to the east and to the north of it, the Switzerland of Canada, the Eastern Townships of the Province of Quebec, one of the counties of which I have the honour to represent in this House. There is no more charming part of Canada than the Eastern Townships. Lake, river, mountain, forest and fertile field all combine in a most pleasant variety to make this the most beautiful district of Canada in the minds of a great many thinking Canadians. I know that other members think that they represent the most beautiful counties in Canada, but I challenge comparison with the Eastern Townships for beauty of scenery, salubrity of climate, and purity of -water.
I accept my hon. friend's challenge. It is well known that the Gatineau is the Switzerland of Canada.
What about the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency for scenic beauty?
The Gatineau may be described as the Tyrol of Canada,* but the Eastern Townships are our Switzerland.
What about Nova Scotia?

Nova Scotia no doubt has also many beautiful spots. As a matter of fact Canada is replete with beautiful

spots. The leader of the Opposition and the members for Queen's will declaim on the beauties of Prince Edward Island, and others will tell us of the beauties of the lower St. Lawrence. Prom the Atlantic to the Pacific Canada is full of natural beauties. But the point I wish to make is that that is an opening for a tremendous development of tourist traffic through the Eastern Townships. We have good railway connection by the Boston and Maine, the Central Vermont and the Canadian Pacific, with the great centres of population not only of our own country but of the United States, and there is a great opportunity for the development of the summer resort business. That being the fact, it is incumbent upon the minister, it seems to me, to open this question again to see whether a mistake has not been made, in order that the fishing in the Mississquoi may be improved. That the member for Mississquoi (Mr. Kay) and myself, from the information we have at our disposal, believe that it was a mistake to prohibit seine fishing, and that the removal of the rough fish in the lake will result in the amelioration of
the conditions for game fish.

and substituting therefor the words:
Acts respecting Food and Drugs andi Honey and Maple Products.

Why amend the i^em
at this stage?	,

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amendment is quite within the rules. There is no change in the destination of the funds, but since these Estimates were framed the Acts in question have been amended and are known by different names, and this is simply for the purpose of substituting the new names of those Acts.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is an
increase of $20,000 over last year. How does that become necessary?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The increased estimate is due to two causes. First, it is intended to provide for the establishment in the city of Montreal of one of the small laboratories which we use in the Food Adulteration Branch. At the present time we have laboratories in Winnipeg, Halifax and Vancouver, and it has been found desirable to have one at Montreal. A number of cases have arisen within the last year where it was important to have an examination of the samples of food taken, and in order to have such examination it is necessary in the interests of the proper enforcement of the law to have a small laboratory available in Montreal. Its estimated cost is $10,000. The other increase is due to larger amounts necessary to provide for the pay of the inspectors appointed under the Act for the enforcement of the law. Unfortunately during the past year a number of these men have resigned because they did not feel the compensation was adequate, and in replacing them we have had to pay larger remuneration.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Were the new ones appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. Then there were also some giving part time to the Inland Revenue and part time to the food administration. They resigned their positions as inspectors under these Acts and are devoting their whole time to Inland Revenue work. The increased duties under these Acts will require the whole time of the new men appointed. These men will not only have their duties as inspectors under the Act relating to Food and Drugs, but they will also have to render assistance in enforcing the provisions of the Proprietary and Patent Medicine Act and the Opium and Narcotic Drugs Act.
Will the minister give the names of the food inspectors in Nova Scotia and their salaries?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Halifax, R. J. Waugh.
He has been receiving $1,250. It is considered that his salary should be increased, and this will be done if the commission approves.

Is he still Deputy Inspector
of Weights and Measures?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. He is now become
solely an inspector under these Acts.

But he has been Deputy
Inspector of Weights and Measures?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know. I know some of these men did work under the Inland Revenue Act and under this Act, but in future they are working solely under these Acts. This man was paid under this Act before, so I assume he must have given his whole time to it. At Sydney, E, T. MacKeen, salary $1,200. Those are the only two in the province of Nova Scotia.

Who is the inspector
at Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: E: T. MacKeen.
Is he not an officer of the Inland Revenue Department?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He would be under the

Then, when the administration of the Act was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce he became an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce and was one of the officials transferred to this Department when the admins-tration of the Adulteration of Foods Act came under the Department of Health.

I think my hon.
friend's history of Mr. MacKeen's position is altogether wrong. He was appointed as Collector of Inland Revenue at Sydney some years ago, Mr. Fraser, of Pictou, was the chief officer of the Department in that part of Canada and Mr. MacKeen was second to him, I understand. I believe that a change has been made in his position.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He may have been originally appointed as Collector of Inland Revenue but more recently he has been devoting his whole time to work connected with the enforcement of this Act.
Formerly there was an officer an the county of Antigonish who received a small salary under the title of Food Inspector. Is that office still in existence?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have no such officer there at the present time.

There
are not two classes of food inspectors

one class under another department, perhaps?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.
What is Mr. Waugh's salary?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
I know Mr Waugh very well, though he is a resident < f Halifax. For a

number of years he has visited Lunenburg and other counties on the western shore of the province. A man of his ability is certainly entitled to much more than $1,250 a year. I do not know how he can live in Halifax on that salary. If the Civil Service classification gives him only that amount, the minister should see that these officials are properly paid.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is my intention to recommend that four inspectors who have been a long time in the service at important centres be classified as senior inspectors and receive $1,680 a year. Mr. Waugh is one of them.
Who are the others?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The others are at Montreal, Toronto and Winnipeg respectively.
What is Mr. MacKeen's salary?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
I certainly thought that Mr. MacKeen was getting a larger salary than that. Mr. MacKeen does not live in my riding, nor is he on my side of politics; nevertheless I say of him that there is not a more efficient officer in Canada. He is a scholarly man, fairly well up in years and cannot give his attention to anything other than the business of the Government, in which he has been engaged for a long time. It is absolutely impossible for him to live in Sydney on a salary of $1,200; he could not rent a respectable house and provide the other necessaries of life for that amount. If the department expects to retain the services of Mr. MacKeen they should give him more than $1,200. It would be much kinder to say to him:	"We will not keep you;
we will dispense with your service," and thus allow him to do something else, rather than keep him at a salary upon which it is impossible for a man of his position and standing to live in Sydney, where it is just as expensive to live as in Ottawa, Montreal or Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All these salaries, of
course, are supplemented by a bonus. Mr. MacKeen, I suppose, is a married man?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then he would get in addition to his salary a bonus of $420. The classification of the Department of Health has not yet been completed. Without a doubt the four inspectors whom I have mentioned should receive increases of salary to the extent that I have suggested;

the other salaries will be under review when the commission takes up the application of the classification to these positions.

If Mr. MacKeen were getting $1,600 with $400 bonus he would be getting $2,000 a year. Well, that is not a fat salary for a married man who has to keep house in Sydney. No matter how much we are pressing for economy just now along every line it is not right to ask men of Mr. MacKeen's attainments to work for less than $2,000 a year, particularly when they have to live where prices are at top-notch.

What
are these officers doing? The present Government kept in office for some years in my county an inspector who really had nothing to do; he had no food to inspect except that contained in the porridge pot in his own kitchen. He received a small salary from the Government just the same.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That must be the one
that has disappeared.

I am
pleased to hear that the office has disappeared. I congratulate the minister on taking that step. I stand for economy, and anything like that is so rare on the part of this Administration that I think I ought to speak about it. What about the second part of this item, administration of the Act respecting fertilizers?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
An amendment struck
that out. The Commercial Feeding Stuffs Act and the Fertilizers Act are now under the Department of Agriculture.
My hon. friend has retained supervision over the bees, if I mistake not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They are still here.
Do I understand the minister to say that he intends to appoint new officials. If so, how does he intend to appoint them?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is no intention of appointing officials where we have not had officials in the past; but as I explained in answer, I think, to the leader of the Opposition, some officials have retired, and we have not so far succeeded in getting persons to fill their places. Appointments will be made by the Civil Service Commission who have been asked to advertise for and secure the additional men needed. We contemplate 25 inspectors for the whole of Canada.

My experience of the Civil Service Commission is that they do not
know their business, and the sooner we repeal the Civil Service Act, the better for the country. I should like to know how the minister satisfies himself that the Civil Service 'Commission can appoint at Halifax or Vancouver a suitable man, say in connection with adulteration of food. My opinion is that the minister or his deputy head can do better in that regard than the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a question of
policy which has been deeded already; it is the whole question of the patronage system or the Civil Service Commission. I do not think it is profitable to enter into that question to-night, and I do not think it is germane to this issue. From my experience of appointments, I may say that on the whole the Civil Service Commission is doing very well in that regard, and I believe they have made exceedingly good appointments, where they have made them so far, in the Department of Health.

My criticism of the whole of this item is that it looks very much as if the minister were struggling to find something for this new department to do. I never saw such a mixture before-adulteration of food, proprietary or patent medicines, housing, bees, pollution of boundary waters,, marine hospitals, quarantine, immigration and medical inspection, research and venereal diseases. These are various things that are collected together in order to make an excuse for a new department which is to be called a Department of Health, presided over by.a minister with a salary of $7,000, a deputy with a salary of $5,000, and a large number of officials under them who, to my mind, are not needed at all. It strikes me that the mixture which is to be found in this item is pretty good proof that there was no necessity for building up this big administration, and these things are gathered together as an excuse for spending a great deal of money in a new department. Formerly,. the business of this country was done by about fourteen departments. I do not know how many there are now; but I think there is an increase of about 50 per cent in the number of departments, and I hope we are going to find the end of that pretty soon. It is quite proper that there should be some one to look after health matters; but I do not think it was at all necessary that there should be a Department of Health, a very expensive machinery built up for that purpose. This work could
[DOT]3542

have been done in some other way, perhaps by having a head under some minister as is the case in many other departments, without incurring .so much expense as we seem to be incurring here. We are taking small items away from other departments and placing them under this one, in order apparently to build up a new department at an enormous expense to the country.
Proprietary or patent medicines, $10,000.
What is this for?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is to make the necessary provision for carrying out the Act passed last session relating to proprietary and patent medicines, and this Act, as my hon. friends will recall, imposed some very important restrictions in connection with the sale of proprietary or patent medicines, particularly as to the character of the drugs that might be contained in them, prohibiting the use of opium and other narcotic drugs in certain preparations. It also provided for the creation of an advisory board to settle certain matters arising under the Act, and the additiohal amount is to cover both these items. As a matter of fact,, under the Act, provision is made for charging a fee for each patent of proprietary medicine registered under the Act, and the proprietor must take out an annual license for its sale. It is considered, in fixing the fee, that sufficient revenue should be derived to pay the cost of administration; that is the basis upon which the Act ii being worked out, so that I do not anticipate any more will be spent than the amount actually received from the druggists of the country for the licenses which they must take out.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The increase

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that we are putting into force a new Act, new in the character of its requirements from the druggists of the Dominion. It is difficult to say what the exact cost of administration will be. I hope it will not reach $10,000; but we have no other means of getting funds to provide for the administration of the Act than by coming down to Parliament and asking for an appropriation. Therefore, >ve have inserted in the Estimates a sum which we believe will be amply sufficient. On the other hand, we are making provision to secure, through the

license fees charged under the Act, a revenue which we believe will fully offset the expenditure. Let me give simply one item. The members of the Advisory Board, which is being constituted from amongst the foremost physicians and pharmacists of this country, are each paid an annual fee of $500 and their travelling expenses in coming to Ottawa to attend meetings of the board. Under the Act of last, session, they have certain very important functions to perform, one of which is to determine the degree of medication necessary in drugs containing alcohol, to prevent their use as an alcoholic stimulant and to make them properly medicines and not liquids sold as a beverage. Under the Act as passed, this board is given final authority to determine that, and it is a matter of pharmaceutical or chemical skill to determine it. That is one very important function they have been asked to perform and they have already been called upon to determine that in the case of a number of patent and proprietary medicines. In addition, there is a whole list of drugs named in the schedule to the Proprietary or Patent Medicines Act the use of which may be deleterious to health and yet the use of which in limited quantities under certain conditions may be beneficial. The board are the final authority to pass upon what quantities of these scheduled drugs may be used in any patent- or proprietary medicine. Hon. members will see that they are called upon' to perform important duties, and we have chosen the best men in Canada for that position.

Who are the .members of that board?
,Mr. ROWELL:	The board consists of
Dr. A. Blackader; Dr. Chas. F. Heebner, of the College of Pharmacy at Toronto; Dr. R. D. Rudolph; Professor J. E, Jiecours,-and 'Dr. A. McGill. Professor Lecours is of Laval University, I think, and Dr. Blackader of McGill.
What about Dr. Rudolph?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is of Toronto.
A strange name for Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He is a good man notwithstanding the name. We have secured some of the best experts in Canada to deal with these particular problems, and the board as -named is, I think, the strongest we can secure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How were they appointed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By Order -in Council under the Act.	i

Will this
money all be spent at the head office?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, in so far as it is
spent.
It strikes me that this item should appear as salaries instead of "proprietary or patent medicines..'

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is not for salaries. The salaries of the officers who administer the Act come under Civil Government. These are expenses incidental to the administration of the Act. In addition to the advisory board to the members of which we pay $500 a year, plus travelling expenses, we have the travelling expenses of the officials in the administration of the Act. Stationery also constitutes an important item under this Act. License foirms and circulars have to be sent out in large numbers, particularly in bringing into operation a new Act about which there is a certain amount of misunderstanding, and where you must be in constant communication with all the druggists throughout Canada, of whom there are thousands. This item is to cover all expenses of this character.
As the minister is such a great believer in the Civil Service Commission, why did not the commission appoint the Advisory Board?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Because the Act provided they should be appointed by the Governor in Council.
Then why does the Act go outside the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not responsible for the framing of the Act. It was the Act I was called upon to administer.
In other words, the minister is "passing the buck"?
Was this Act passed before the minister was joined by the President of the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it was passed last session.
Has not the minister to share responsibility for the Act with his colleagues?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Absolutely.
Why not answer my question? Why were they appointed by Order in Council instead of by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Because the Act so
provides.
That is not a proper answer.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a good one.

I thought that every appointment within the power of the Government, even to the staff of the House of Commons, was, after the passing of the Civil Service Act, to be made by the Civil Service Commission. I thought the Civil Service Act overrode every provision in every other statute passed before that Act which gave any man or minister power to appoint. That was the intention, as expressed by the members of the Government and all those who defended the Civil Service Act when it was before the House.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is evidently " under a misapprehension. These men are not officials of the Government; they are not members of the Civil Service. They are simply appointed to this board because of their professional skill to settle certain! technical matters connected with the administration of thic Act, for which they are paid a fee fixed at $500.
It is a salary.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it is a fee of $500, We decided that was a fair fee for their professional services given as members of this board.

I do not object to the appointment of these men, but I object to some officials being appointed by Order in Council and others by the Civil Service Commission when the Government wants to "pass the buck". My idea is that all officials should be appointed by responsible heads, not by this farce down town in the Hunter Building called the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
