speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount expended last year was approximately $20,000, which came out of the demobilization vote. The Government's housing policy was part of the programme of re-establishment of returned soldiers, and it consisted in making provision for loaning $25,000,000 to the provincial governments to enable them to make advances to municipalities and individuals for the erection of houses. The Government did not charge against the municipalities the cost of administration so far as the Federal Government itself was concerned. It provided that money, and provided it out of the demobilization vote, because the Government believed it related to the re-settlement and re-establishment of our returned men, and therefore fairly came within the scope of the demobilization vote. We could have taken a special vote for it last year, but that was not done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why does this come under the Department of Health, instead of under Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Because housing has a very close relationship to health and was being administered by a committee of the Cabinet, of which I happened to be the chairman. Therefore, when the Department of Health was formed, it was intimated to the House at the time that housing would probably be assigned to that department. Housing comes under the Department of Health in Great Britain. They recognize that good housing bears so close a relationship to the physical and social welfare of the people that it constitutes a proper branch of the Department of Health, and so in Canada, as in these other countries,, it comes under this department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Can the minister give us some details of this expenditure? Who are the salaried officials and what is the nature of the general expenses in the administration of this Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The chief officer administering the housing regulations of the Government has been Mr. Adams, the Town Planning Expert of the Commission of Conservation, but he was not paid anything extra for this work. The salary he received from the Conservation Commission, as their Town Planning Adviser, covered his services to us in administering the housing regulations. Mr. Adams had to have assistance in carrying on his work-two expert helpers, an engineer and an architect, and also the necesfMr. Mackenzie King.]
sary office staff. The expenditure referred to covers the salaries of his assistants.
How were they appointed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They were all appointed through the Civil Service Commission, or transferred from some other department. I think one was transferred from the Department of the Interior and the others were appointed by the commission.

The explanation given by the minister would seem to show that this money was voted out for the year ending March 31, 1920. We are now voting money for the current year 19201921. Do I understand the minister to say that he took the $15,000 out of the demobilization vote of last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What I said was that the expense of administering these regulations last year was paid out of the demobilization vote. We are asking this year for a vote to cover the expenses of carrying out this service.
Where is that mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is only mentioned as
an explanation to show where the money came from last year.

That
does not refer to housing.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You have in the estimates one column of figures for 1920-21 and another for 1919-20. There is no item opposite housing in 1919-20. In the absence of an explanation it would appear that it wias an entirely new vote. There was an expenditure last year and the note is simply to explain where the money came from.

That is
a very indirect way of explaining it. Are there any other expenditures that were taken from the demobilization vote of last year.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are all kinds of
expenditures, as the statement submitted to the House at the time the demobilization vote was granted would indicate. I have not the figures before me but my hon. friend will recollect that when the demobilization vote was asked by the Prime Minister, or the Finance Minister, he submitted a statement setting out in detail the various departments of the Government or the various classes of services to which the moneys voted might be expected to be applied.
For war purposes?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For the purpose stated by the Government.
Anything could be taken out of it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, because the Auditor General would see to it 'that no payment was taken out of that vote that did not come within the terms of the Act.

I do not think the Government have any right to take this money out of the demobilization vote because this is not for war purposes. I have a very strong suspicion that if we had all the Orders in Council passed by the Government during this last year we would find a number of similar inroads made upon the demobilization vote. The minister ought to furnish us with the information before we go very much farther. it came to my knowledge g few days ago that a news agency had been started in the city of New York that had nothing whatever to do with the demobilization of soldiers or with the war, and yet it is paid for, by Order in Council, out of the demobilization vote. That is a very improper thing to do. Such a direct violation of the statute cannot be justified. If the expense of a news agency started after the war is over in order to provide a job for a needy supporter, is to be taken out of the demobilization vote, see where we will land. If the' Government can dip into the demobilization vote for any expenditure which is not authorized by Parliament we have come to a pretty pass in these matters. I think the minister, before he asks us to pass this item, ought to furnish the Committee with all the Orders in Council that, have been inroads upon the demobilization vote for various purposes and in the different departments. Without that we will not be able to know where we are in regard to this vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry I cannot
agree with the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Sinclair). I do not think the demobilization vote of last year and the appropriation of all the moneys provided for by that vote are relevant to the item under' discussion at the present time.

We are discussing item

Housing-salaries and general expenses, expenditure 1919-1920, from Demobilization Appropriation Act, $15,000.

If I understand aright this year is 1920-21 and this amount is taken from the demobilization appropriation. The position taken by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is absolutely right. Demobilization is a part of the war legislation when this housing scheme came before the House I opposed it and criticised it on the ground, first, that the Government had no right to lend money to richer people than themselves and, second, that if they undertook to give any assistance towards building houses they should do it for soldiers alone and not for the general public. I do not think you can properly charge this expenditure to the demobilization vote. I do not care what the Department of Public Health, the Prime Minister or anybody else says, I maintain this has nothing whatever'to do with the war. Tt is not right that demobilization and the war should be charged with the cost of a policy initiated by the Government in expectation of an election to try and gain popularity in the various provinces more especially as this expenditure was an uncalled for extravagance considering the financial position of the country. The Government loaned money to the provinces without any justification whatever. I do not see how we can camouflage this policy any longer by charging the war, war loans and Victory loans with money the Government desires to spend to create some popularity in the provinces. The position taken by the hon. member for Guysborough I think is absolutely sound, and that we ought to have some further explanation about this expenditure. Money voted for demobilization should not be paid to cover up the extravagance of the Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Explanations concerning this item are in order but not all expenditures under the demobilization vote of last year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask the minister if he has information to show what proportion of these houses have been constructed in rural areas and what proportion in urban areas?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These have all been constructed in urban areas, or in districts immediately adjacent to urban areas. The regulations do not contemplate the erection of houses on farms for farm labourers, if that is what my hon. friend has in view.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What I have in view is this: These Estimates relate to the Health Department, I feel very strongly that the encouragement of buildings in cities, as against the encouragement of buildings in rural areas, is a tendency in the wrong direction, and it is one that the 
Minister of Health in particular ought to take into consideration. I do not know what the opinion of my hen. frien/d is- I would like to get it from him- as to whether or not it is in the national interest to encourage the construction of buildings in urban areas as against the construction off /buildings in rural areas. All these millions that have been voted have apparently gone to the construction of buildings in urban areas, thus encouraging the population to further congest the crowded centres which I think is detrimental to the health of the people, a fact which should be the primary consideration of this department.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We' were facing a condition and not a theory. The situation we faced was that there was a shortage of houses in urban centres when our soldiers returned to Canada. These regulations were intended to aid in relieving the congestion in the cities due to the large additional demand for houses caused by the return of our soldiers from overseas, and the fact that there had been relatively little house-building done during the war. The regulations were not intended to apply to rural areas. If a shortage of buildings exists in the rural areas it is a matter that the provinces can very well deal with. Under these regulations the buildings must be of a sanitary character, of a certain size, and possess sufficient light and air space, drainage, and all the conditions which make for a good, healthy, comfortable home at the cheapest possible cost.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My criticism
is that the Government by making these loans applicable exclusively to the urban centres is encouraging a possible tendency which should be well considered. I think we ought to consider very carefully, before we vote additional loans, whether we should encourage this tendency of the movement of the people to the cities at the expense of the country. I notice that in the miscellaneous items, No. 318, there is a loan of $25,000,000 to Provincial Governments to engage in the erection of houses on the terms and conditions set forth in the Order in Council. [DOT] I presume it is the administration of that amount twhich is being covered by the item No. 63 we are now considering. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is not a new vote.
The $25,000,000 is the vote of last year. The Dominion Government granted this sum as a loan to the provinces, in proportion to their population for the purpose I have
\

mentioned. This year we are simply providing for a re-vote of that portion of it which the provinces were not in a position to avail themselves of last year. Some of them were late in getting their housing plans under way, and did not ask for an advance last year. From others we received exceedingly strong recommendations that a larger sum should be voted this year in view of the growing demand for accommodation in the cities and towns. According to the opinion of some hon. members the Government went too far in voting the $25,000,000 referred to.
I think it was a measure designed in the public interest which will ameliorate the existing conditions and help considerably towards the betterment of the housing situation.

As a matter of fact, it is
said that a great many of these houses are merely summer cottages built for people wrho already possess houses in the cities.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that any such houses have been built. If any such dwellings have been constructed it would be contrary to the purpose for which the money was granted and a violation of the terms on which the money was loaned to the province.
There should be a statement by the Government setting forth the conditions under which the money is loaned by the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The provinces are the
borrowers of the money. They are the ones that must lay down the conditions' under which the loans are made. All that we require is that those conditions shall not be contrary to but in conformity with the general regulations which this Government has laid down in order to secure the kind of houses that I have referred to. Beyond that the provinces themselves take the responsibility, and we have not felt it necessary to do other than require reports from them. We have their obligation to repay us and we run no risk except that we loan them the money at >5 per cent-that is our contribution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In fixing the conditions under which the loans are made I think it would be wise to provide that the provinces should see that a certain percentage of the money is spent on cottages or houses in rural areas as well as in urban areas. Does the minister think it wise to permit public funds to be used exclusively for the purpose of erecting dwellings in urban centres?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the provinces are perfectly competent to do that for themselves. I do not think we should undertake it. At the present time there is a large demand for houses in the cities and towns throughout Canada, and the provinces are making these loans for the purpose of meeting an actual condition of serious congestion which exists. If people cannot get homes to live in they are crowded in flats and tenements and we will be duplicating to a limited extent the slum conditions of the Old Country. In so far as we can relieve the situation, it is our duty to do so, and that is the most pressing and urgent need. If the provinces consider it desirable to assist in the construction of dwellings in the country they have a perfect right to do so, using their own money for the purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If the minister wants to eliminate the crowding, and possibly the creation of slums, in the cities, he will accept my suggestion. As it is, it seems to me that the Government's policy is going to encourage the building of houses in the cities rather than in the rural areas, and promote the tendency of the population to drift toward the urban centres. While the Government apparently has not any policy on the high cost of living, I think it might very well take this aspect of the question into consideration when making loans from the treasury.

The Act now works against the rural areas because there is no method by which a farmer under this system can borrow money to build a house. In the first place, as I understand it, the Dominion Government lend the money to the Provincial Government, and the latter lends it to the city, and the city in turn lends it to the builder of the house and takes security for the loan. But a farmer living in a country district where there is no machinery to deal with a third party has no chance to get a loan at all. The difficulty is inherent in the system devised by the Government, which is a system to build up the cities at the expense of the country.
How much money was loaned to each province under the scheme last year?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The return I have is made up for the fiscal year ending 31st of March last. British Columbia. $750,000; Man!

toba, $1,580,000; New Brunswick, $1,220,000; Ontario, $8,750,000; Quebec, $60,000. The amounts were advanced as each province submitted its housing plan, had it approved, and requested the advance.
In what urban centres in the province of Quebec has advantage been taken of the Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no statement showing that information.
Have not various demands been made by each province under agreement with the Government?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The amount which each province is to receive under the agreement with the Government has already been intimated by the Government to the Provincial Governments; it is the percentage which the population of each province bears to the total population of Canada on the basis of the census of 1911. On that basis so soon as a province submits its housing scheme and has it approved, it is entitled to advances just as it requests them. We do not exercise any detailed supervision as to when the advances should be made. The province of Quebec had its scheme approved, but it requested only $60,000 before the close of the last fiscal year.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that if a province submitted a plan to advance money for the building of houses in rural districts the federal authorities could approve it?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the housing plan complied with the general regulations laid down by the Government upon which Parliament
voted the money, yes; that is all we require.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the minister the terms and conditions of the Order in Council of December 3, 1918?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have the Order here. It provides:
That the aggregate amount to be loaned to all provinces shall not exceed $25,0'00i,00'0, and the amount of loan to any one province shall not exceed the proportion of the said $25,000,000 which the population of the said province bears to the total population of Canada.
That the loans made hereunder may be for a period not exceeding twenty years, with the right to any province to pay off the whole or any part of the principal of the loan at any time during the said term.
I presume that the clause my hon. friend has in mind is the condition upon which advances may be made, which is No. 7:
Advances may be made as soon as a general scheme of housing shall have been agreed upon 
between the Government of Canada and the Government of the province applying for a loan hereunder.
Under that Order in Council a set of general regulations was prepared setting out the principles which should be applied in
the construction of homes to be aided by this loan. These general regulations were submitted to all the provinces for their consideration and comment, and they were advised that if they (lid not make any suggestions they would be deemed to have approved the regulations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where is the general scheme to be found?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is all printed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is that you have in your hand?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have here the general regulations covering the Housing project of the Federal Government, printed last session by order of the House, and distributed. Certain suggestions were made by some of the provinces, which if of any importance were given effect to, but they were of minor character in any case. So we had a general scheme agreed upon between the Federal Government and the provincial governments which was embodied in a further Order in Council. Then each province in turn prepared its scheme. It was at liberty to add any provision to these general regulations which it thought necessary in the interest of the province. British Columbia, I think, limited its grants to returned soldiers. I do not recall that any other province did so.
Would not the loan of $8,750,000 to Ontario be about its quota?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it is probably very near it. If it is its quota, then Ontario cannot have any more. My hon. friend will see that when we come to the re-vote, the proportion, of the loan not taken up, it is available only upon the conditions of the original grant, and to the provinces which have not yet taken full advantage of the loan.
What does the minister mean by the 4,000 houses proposed to be built in Ontario? Where will the money come from for those houses?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Ontario did what none of the other provinces did,-added of its own provincial funds $2,000,000 to the amount loaned by the Federal Government. The whole of this amount has not so far been advanced by Ontario to the

municipalities. The province has borrowed funds from us for this purpose. Housing plans have been formulated by the different municipalities to put up the houses to which I made reference, and the amount will be advanced 'by the province to the municipalities as they comply with the provincial regulations. If there is not a sufficient sum available from the federal loan to complete those houses, the province must advance the money itself. The provincial government has passed an 'Act authorizing the guarantee of the bonds of municipalities for the purpose of erecting additional houses. The movement thus started in Ontario has developed such momentum that although the province cannot get further financial assistance from us, it is cooperating with the municipalities to provide the necessary funds to put up a Targe number of additional houses.
Do I understand that half the cost of the 4,000 houses projected for Ontario is paid by Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No. Our information
from Ontario is that they are putting up a certain amount in connection with the loans to municipalities. We have not stipulated for it; it is no part of our undertaking; it is purely voluntary on their part.

What I want to get at is where the money is coming from for these -4,000 houses? My hon. friend is taking credit for the results of the expenditure of last year. He says that 1,184 houses were built; how much money was spent?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
stop to think he will realize that where you are advancing money to a province and the province is advancing money to a municipality you do not have the houses all completed as of a certain date. Housing schemes are under way; plans are developing; certain houses are completed from month to month; others are in course of [DOT]construction; in other cases the ground is just being cleared. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
General regulations as
framed between the Federal and Provincial Governments provided different prices for different classes of houses. It has been found necessary this year, on urgent representation from the provinces, by reason of the increased cost of building, to raise these figures to $3,500 and $4,000 respectively.

Taking the average cost
of the house as only $3,000, the 4,000 houses projected in Ontario would involve an expenditure of $12,000,000, whereas Ontario has been advanced only $8,000,000. I do not get my hon. friend's point; he seems to be taking credit for something he is not doing. He claims that a great many houses have been built throughout the country, but we learn that the number completed is 1,180- about the number of houses built during the same period in the suburb of a second or third-class city in Canada. Apparently the provinces, outside of Ontario, are not asking for this money. The minister tells us about" the wonderful things that are being done in Ontario in the house-building line, but he is making no provision for the furnishing of any more money. Not only the members of the Opposition, but, I am sure, Parliament and certainly the people of Canada are getting tired of the minister's misstatements.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member knows that the statement he has made is untrue. I have not misstated any matter to the committee. My hon. friend repeatedly gets up, though, and does make misstatements. He surely should have some respect for the honour of a member of Parliament.
What misstatement did I make. I ask the minister to mention one misstatement that I made.

speechtext: I could not reflect on my hon. friend's

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not given any decision yet, but at prsent I cannot see my way clear to give an affirmative answer. I have not yet finally disposed of it, but that is the situation up to date. My difficulty lies in establishing a new precedent, which would be quoted in all sections of the country where similar grants would be urged. My hon. friend knows haw strongly, the shipowners are protesting against the existing tax. If we go on making grants for building hospitals, I am afraid we cannot limit it to the port my hon. friend mentions. However, I have not finally disposed of the matter, but that is the impression I have up to date.

I think the minister could overcome the difficulty he mentions by imposing a similar liability on the town that makes the application. You would not have many applications if the town making the application was required to contribute a similar amount. If we are going to collect this tax from the ships in this country, we ought/ to assume the duty of providing for the sailors. We are not doing it at the present time. In certain places there is no provision made for taking care of sick sailors. The British system, which has been suggested by my hon. friend
(Mr. Stevens), is much better than ours. Under the British system the British Consul in any part of the world assumes the responsibility of taking care of a sick sailor. He sends him to a hospital, and looks after him. If the sailor is not able to join his ship the Consul pays his fare to England or wherever he belongs. The bill comes from the British Consul at that foreign port to the Board of Trade in England, and the Board of Trade transmits it to the Minister of Marine in Canada, who transmits it to the owner of the ship who has to pay it. So the sailor is looked after in every case. Under our system we are collecting large sums of money from the ships, but we are not assuming the responsibility of taking care of the sick sailors. In the town I refer to there is no hospital within many miles to take care of sick sailors. The sailors are put ashore, and' for anything the department has to do with them they may die on the shore because there is no place to which they can go. This is a system which should not continue. The department, if they will not do any work at all, should abolish this tax alto-gather or they should assume responsibility for taking care of the sick. This is trust money that the minister is collecting from the ships. When the minister takes the surplus of this money and puts it into the consolidated revenue fund he is- not doing right if the sailors are not looked after. They are not looked after. I could give instances where men have lost their lives because there is no provision made for taking care of them at distant places where no hospitals exist. Ilf we are to continue this system of collecting from the ships on the coast of this country we must assume the responsibility of taking care of the men.

speechtext:

speechtext:

gentleman the information to-night, but I will look it up and let him have it.

Research-maintenance, replacements, supplies and assistance for a research laboratory, $10,000.
Has this any relation to the work of the Bureau of Research?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No; it deals with a wholly different subject. This is intended to be the initiation of a research laboratory under the Department of Health, which is one of the things most urgently needed in Canada. At the present time we have no adequate provision for this class of work. Take the situation which at present exists: we had throughout Canada during the past six or eight months what was commonly designated as sleeping sickness, but which was not sleeping sickness. Medical men at present do not know the origin of this disease, its method of propagation or its cure, but we do know that it exists, and we know its fatal consequences. We have had the most careful investigations of these cases made by the most skilled medical men, but we have not got a laboratory to-day under the control of the department in which we can follow up these investigations. I hope that we may have established in this capital city a medical research laboratory which will be a credit to the Dominion of Canada, and will encourage scientific

research in those branches so vital to human progress and human welfare. This vote is merely to make possible the initiation of the work.
Venereal Diseases, $200,000.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is to provide for cooperation with the provinces in carrying on a campaign against venereal diseases. We have worked out an arrangement with all the provinces for a united compaign. I may say that one of the best things we have done under the Act providing for the creation of a Department of Health, has been the appointment, of the Dominion Council of Health. The Council consists off the chief executive officers of Health of each of the provinces, plus five others' representing the various civilian, activities in the country, and is presided over by the Deputy Minister of Health as chairman. In consultation with the representatives of the provinces we have worked out an arrangement whereby the provinces undertake to carry out an active compaign against venereal diseases on lines, which have been agreed upon as the result of a consultation of the officers of the department and the chief medical officers of the provinces at the Dominion Council of Health. The provinces agree to put up dollar for dollar in connection with this compaign, and I laid on the table of the House the other day the Order in Council which indicated the distribution of the grant last year. It is on the basis of population, and all the provinces have joined in - the agreement which has been .made for carrying on this united Compaign. The late Si-r William Osier has stated-perhaps in as terse and forcible language as could be expressed-that gonorrhoea is the sterilizer of the race, while syphilis is the killer. These facts in possession of the Department of Health indicate that this campaign is needed in Canada as similar campaigns are needed elsewhere.

voted last year, but the full amount has not been advanced. If we did not re-vote the balance it would permit the provinves which took advantage last year to get the full benefit and the others would get nothing more.
Will the money not taken up by any province be advanced to the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Each province is entitled to its share and no more.

I understand that one
or two provinces have refused to take advantage of this loan?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Alberta is the only one
which so far has not taken advantage of it.	.

Is the money simply
given to the province and distributed as the province sees fit, or have the municipalities anything to do with the scheme?

The grant would lapse, it would not go to the credit of any other province.
To provide for an increase in the salary of the Director-General of Public Health, from the 1st of April, 1919, $1,0'00.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Before this item is considered I would suggest that, inasmuch as item 61, Adulteration of Food, was amended during my temporary absence and does not now apply to the Acts respecting feeding stuffs and fertilizers, the minister might very properly reduce the amount of that item.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would be very glad if I could accommodate my hon. friend, but almost all of the expenditure has been under the Adulteration of Food Acts. Inspectors have been appointed under those Acts, and in addition to their duties they have assisted in the enforcement of the provisions of the Commercial Feeding Stuffs Act and the Act respecting fertilizers. That is the reason that the administration of those Acts was transferred to the Department of Health. They are now transferred to the Department of Agriculture on the understanding that that department has the staff to. enforce them without adding to the public expense. It does not reduce the number of employees required in this department. These employees, however, will have important additional duties this year in connection with the enforcement of the Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act and the Opium and Narcotic Drugs Act.
Does the item we have now reached provide for an increase in salary?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Last year, as hon. mein-bes will recall, all deputy ministers and all other officials who held the rank of deputy minister had their salaries increased from $5,000 to $6,000, with the exception of the Director General of Medical Services. He has served the country for some 54 years and is retiring very shortly. We thought it but right-
Dr. Montizambert?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. We thought it but right that he should be put on the same basis as all other public servants who held the same position last year.
Progress reported.
